### Julian Gewirtz on the realities of AI risk in China [[00:00:00]](https://80000hours.org/podcast/episodes/julian-gewirtz-china-us-ai-deal/?t=0)

**Julian Gewirtz:** We have to start with the reality of what China is and what the Chinese Communist Party cares about, as opposed to kind of working backwards from the place we think they need to get in order to accomplish our broader goals.

The number one concern is regime security, regime stability. As I’ve seen the Chinese AI discourse evolve, there is increasing attention to what they call extreme loss-of-control risks.

The most significant event in shaping the evolution of Beijing’s thinking about AI risks over the course of the past year or so is Mythos.

### What does Xi think of Dario? [[00:00:41]](https://80000hours.org/podcast/episodes/julian-gewirtz-china-us-ai-deal/?t=41)

**Tom Reed:** Today I’m speaking with Julian Gewirtz. Julian is a historian, poet, former director for China affairs in the NSC [National Security Council] under Biden, and more recently also a blogger. Of all the things that I’ve learned from reading [Julian’s work](https://juliangewirtz.substack.com/), perhaps [my favourite](https://www.hup.harvard.edu/books/9780674241848) is that much of the credit we all usually give to Deng Xiaoping for the reform of China’s economy should instead be redirected towards the comparatively uncelebrated former Chinese Premier [Zhao Ziyang](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Zhao_Ziyang). Julian, thank you for coming on the show.

**Julian Gewirtz:** Thanks, Tom. It’s great to be with you.

**Tom Reed:** So, Julian, I have a bunch of not-so-hidden agendas for speaking to you. Above all, I want to understand: what on Earth do you think Xi Jinping’s model of Dario Amodei is? What do you think he thinks this guy wants?

**Julian Gewirtz:** Well, honestly, I don’t think we have to speculate, because to a stunning degree, Beijing has been on the record going after Anthropic. In the history of sort of US–China relations, it’s hard for me to think of another example of an American company that Beijing has taken on so repeatedly and so directly. There have been a series of state media commentaries about it. There was one ahead of Xi Jinping coming to the United States that [I found really striking](https://juliangewirtz.substack.com/p/chinas-ai-reckoning), and [I wrote a little bit about it](https://x.com/JulianGewirtz/status/2094089594828464267), but the headline was “[Anthropic has contracted the American disease](https://www.geopolitechs.org/p/yuyuan-tantian-anthropic-has-caught).”

Now, what does that mean? The core argument was basically that this is a company that says whatever, but is actually all about preserving so-called technological hegemony for the United States. And crucially, we often think about these different AI companies, the different model companies, as very differentiated actors in our system. We know that many of them don’t like each other and that they’re competing intensely, and all of those sort of things that define what it feels like to be in this space.

Beijing said Anthropic is literally “a monster bred by the American path” — saying, like, all of this, all of these different firms, this is all part of one big thing. And that big thing is the United States trying to dominate globally and trying to keep China behind. And they have been going at Anthropic hardest, but they don’t, I think, see it as somehow separate or outside of a mainstream in the United States, but very much a part of it.

And it’s just maybe worth driving home the upshot of that, which is that for Beijing, it appears that a lot of the distinctions or differences in views among American tech titans and American AI companies matter less than what they represent to China, which is the project of American power, in their eyes.

**Tom Reed:** Sometimes I get confused by Dario’s comms on China, because [sometimes](https://darioamodei.com/post/we-must-pace-the-frontier) it sounds like he’s calling for we really need to cooperate with them; [sometimes](https://darioamodei.com/post/on-deepseek-and-export-controls) it sounds like what he’s calling for looks a little bit less like cooperation.

Dario, famously, I think he only has one direct report, which is his chief of staff. But let’s imagine you were his second-ever direct report, and he’d hired you specifically as his China comms person. What would you tell him to say? How should he be talking about China differently in a way that actually increases the chance of them taking his calls seriously, rather than as a call for slowing China down compared to the US?

**Julian Gewirtz:** Well, I guess, honestly, I don’t think it’s very likely that Beijing can somehow be disabused of the notion that the United States wants a significant lead in AI over China. And I don’t think that messaging from any particular executive is going to be the key thing there.

I mean, let’s just step back for a second and say we’re in a moment where the president of the United States has [said](https://finance.yahoo.com/technology/ai/articles/trump-rejects-silicon-valley-calls-165148820.html), “No slowdown. AI risk is not something I want to take seriously.”

**Tom Reed:** “It’s a hoax.”

**Julian Gewirtz:** Sure. And where the secretary of the Treasury has said, “There’s no day after tomorrow if China wins at this.” To the point I was just making, I actually don’t think that they see the rhetoric or comms of one CEO, Dario or otherwise, as the thing that could shift their view.

My own strong view is that the most important thing that could cause Beijing to shift its current approach to AI safety is their own domestic sense of the risks. The second most important thing is if they were to see the United States actually doing AI regulation and taking AI safety seriously — doing basically what we would call a “costly signal,” the kind of thing that we’re doing because we care about these risks, and that also has the benefit of signalling to Beijing, like, “Hey, these guys are serious about this.” Those two things are far more important, I think, than a shift in comms.

I will say I do think that there is a difference between the United States wanting to compete and have a lead, and a narrative of total supremacy, [permanent dominance](https://www.nybooks.com/articles/2026/11/05/the-dream-of-ai-primacy/). So the language, I think, that is least helpful toward getting Beijing there is the language that suggests that what the United States wants here is not just a lead, but total kind of what we would call “primacy.” And there is a distinction there, and I think it is relevant, but all part of a puzzle.

**Tom Reed:** So the idea being that a precondition for China taking any of the US’s apparent AI safety concerns seriously would be: actually regulate AI domestically. Otherwise it just looks like it’s all talk.

**Julian Gewirtz:** Yeah. And obviously that gets us right into the core question of tradeoffs around regulating at home to preserve our edge, and regulating at home with the risk of losing our edge over China. But there, my friend and collaborator [Matt Sheehan](https://carnegieendowment.org/people/matt-sheehan) has a [really good point](https://carnegieendowment.org/emissary/2026/06/trump-ai-order-china-competition), which is that Beijing has itself done some AI regulation at home — not sort of frontier AI risk, but they have deepfake and AI-generated content labelling requirements. They have regulations on chatbots, particularly for minors. They’ve done some stuff there.

And of course we don’t see that as condemning them to be in second place necessarily. In fact, they’re doing all that and we’re still very worried about them catching up to us.

So I think there’s a bit of a fallacy embedded in the idea that any AI regulation is at odds—

**Tom Reed:** Going to lose us the whole race.

**Julian Gewirtz:** Exactly. Now, pacing is a separate question, because that is explicitly about the speed of frontier development. But regulation is a lot more than just pacing.

### Would we ever know about a Chinese Hugging Face hack? [[00:08:27]](https://80000hours.org/podcast/episodes/julian-gewirtz-china-us-ai-deal/?t=507)

**Tom Reed:** How do you think the Chinese government would react to a homegrown version of the [Hugging Face incident](https://80000hours.org/podcast/episodes/hugging-face-hack/)?

**Julian Gewirtz:** Now, in China, I think an incident like that would be seen as a cybersecurity incident first and foremost. And the thing to remember in China is that while the AI regulatory space, and particularly the frontier AI regulatory space, is very much still coming together — and we’ll talk about that, I’m sure — the cybersecurity structures have been in place for a while, and this is a top kind of regime security issue for Beijing.

So I think they’d treat it that way. They do have certain kind of notification requirements where I think the central government could potentially become aware of it pretty quickly. But the most important thing that I think we have to stress is that at every layer, the incentives in that system are not to disclose more information, and certainly not to disclose it publicly.

So the most remarkable thing, as we imagine what a kind of Hugging Face, OpenAI-style incident in China would look like, is the public, I don’t think, would know about it. We might never know about it.

And I think that’s part of the reason why there’s so much concern as we think about these issues. Because in the Chinese political system, whistleblower protections, shall we say, are not something that gets treated with much seriousness. The famous Chinese whistleblowers are people like [the doctor in Wuhan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Li_Wenliang) who warned about the spread of COVID and was punished for that years ago.

So I think anyone at a firm — whether an executive wanting to report up the chain or a whistleblower kind of considering whether to make their concerns known — would be weighing the risk of serious kind of smackdown by the government against the safety risks. And so that’s a pretty challenging place to be.

**Tom Reed:** Interesting. Do you think the government would be fully informed of what happened, or do you think the labs themselves would also be incentivised and capable of hiding such an incident if they became aware of it? I’m just trying to understand exactly who would know if something like this happened.

**Julian Gewirtz:** Well, in an incident like that, where what happened fully escaped the lab’s control and was a third-party website, I think presumably the government would find out that something had occurred, at least via the third-party website. And if there was an investigation, I think some of the labs might be more forthcoming than others.

There is a small chance you could imagine that if they felt they really kind of handled it — and/or if it became publicly known that there had been some sort of hack of this third-party website for other reasons that were visible — I think you could then imagine them doing a very limited kind of disclosure, saying, “There was a problem, we found out about it, we solved it, everything is good, proceed accordingly.”

I think the biggest policy question in Beijing in that kind of moment would be: would something like that trigger what they would call a “broader rectification campaign,” meaning an effort to bring greater control from the central authorities over this area? And that, I think, is possible. But again, it would likely be in a context without the kind of public disclosure that eventually marked the OpenAI Hugging Face incident. And crucially, that [METR report](https://metr.org/blog/2026-08-26-openai-hugging-face-incident-investigation/) — the things that have brought a bit more public confidence back to thinking that at least third-party evaluators have the capacity to inform the public about this — I think highly unlikely in the Chinese case that that would happen.

**Tom Reed:** Is there a particular flavour of near-term AI incident that you think would be more likely to cause something like a broader rectification campaign? What I’m trying to think of is: are there some kinds of ways that AI could go rogue that would be more worrying to the CCP [Chinese Communist Party] than others, or that might encourage them to view things as not just any other familiar cyber incident?

**Julian Gewirtz:** We have to start with the reality of what China is and what the Chinese Communist Party cares about, as opposed to kind of working backwards from the place we think they need to get in order to accomplish our broader goals.

And I say that because the number one concern is regime security, regime stability — what they call political security and social stability. So the kinds of risks that I think are most likely to cause them to recalibrate some of their current approach to the AI sector are really in that domain. They do want to avoid risks to regime security, also sort of major economic disruptions. So from that perspective, I think as we consider the kinds of scenarios that might unfold, it’s really the ones that are in that core political and regime security space.

And as your listeners well know, there are those risks — and in fact, control over information, particularly information about the government, about the Communist Party, access to a very carefully controlled cyber and information ecosystem: that is the kind of thing that we can imagine these new tools, new technologies disrupting, either inadvertently via loss of control by a company, or deliberately. And I think the deliberate piece of this is a big element to just bring in, because candidly, as I have seen the Chinese AI discourse evolve, there is increasing attention to what they call “extreme loss-of-control risks.”

But we have to remember that when they use that phrase, “loss of control,” they don’t simply mean it in the way that a lot of AI safety folks here mean it — loss of human control over AI systems — but also as the loss of political control linked to AI more generally. And so when we think of deliberate hacking, deliberate dissemination of information that the government doesn’t want spread, those are all the kind of risks, I think, that are likely in the first instance to make them really start to reconsider.

And, sorry, maybe just one last thing, but there was recently this vulnerability exposed—

**Tom Reed:** This is [the hack of WeChat](https://www.nytimes.com/2026/09/11/world/asia/china-ai-attack-wechat.html)?

**Julian Gewirtz:** Yeah, exactly. The vulnerability in WeChat, which is the sort of One App to Rule Them All in China.

**Tom Reed:** So just to clarify for our audience: this was a hack of WeChat that was disclosed by a group that had used AI to find the vulnerability. They’d found a vulnerability, but they disclosed it responsibly. But we have no idea exactly how the government sort of processed this information. We just know that it happened and they would be aware of it.

**Julian Gewirtz:** Right. And sort of in line with what we were just saying a second ago, the response of Tencent, the company that created WeChat, was to say, “We patched the vulnerability.” But the shoe that never dropped publicly was how the government saw that and what kind of conversations about the vulnerability there were.

But there was just one other thing which I should have said in the prior set of comments, which is: the US factor here is major. And I think in a way, the most significant event in shaping the evolution of Beijing’s thinking about AI risks over the course of the past year or so is [Mythos](https://80000hours.org/podcast/episodes/claude-mythos-hacking-alignment/) — and the kind of sense that the United States is gaining extraordinary capabilities in cyber. And that that is motivating a set of counter-responses that we have very little visibility into, but that they see as part of the AI risk conversation centrally. And whenever they talk about AI risk at the government level or the party level, they talk about the United States as one of the threats.

**Tom Reed:** It’s like the main risk for them is US primacy through AI advantages or something like that?

**Julian Gewirtz:** I still think loss of political control, political security, is number one. But a very close second is the US dimension, exactly as you say. And crucially, they’re connected.

**Tom Reed:** And how do we know that Mythos was this sort of wake-up call for them? I’ve heard this before, but how is it that we know this is the case? They’ve not said, “Oh, this was a wakeup call for us.” Are there signs that Mythos shifted things for the CCP?

**Julian Gewirtz:** No, I don’t think any government would call a press conference and say, “We’re really freaked out about this.” But no, there are a few things.

First, there are indications in official statements where they have quite directly invoked it. So they have spoken about it a little bit. They don’t say, “We’ve turned up the alarm to the highest level,” but they acknowledge the reality of it, and they acknowledge it as something that could pose a kind of security set of challenges for China. And then second, in [track II dialogues](https://www.opb.org/article/2026/09/19/when-trump-and-xi-meet-they-will-discuss-ai-track-two-talks-are-already-buzzing/) and other settings where there’s communication, it’s been quite clear that this is something that has reverberated profoundly in their system.

And in general, to go back to that initial point of starting from what China is and what the party cares about, their concern about American cyber capabilities and all the rest has been a huge issue for well over a decade. Xi Jinping has spoken about this frequently over the years. So they are primed to see that as a threat vector of the greatest significance.

### How Beijing views distillation [[00:18:56]](https://80000hours.org/podcast/episodes/julian-gewirtz-china-us-ai-deal/?t=1136)

**Tom Reed:** Can I force you to make a guess about something?

**Julian Gewirtz:** Sure. You’re not going to necessarily be able to force me, but you can try.

**Tom Reed:** I could try, I could try. And yeah, to clarify for our audience, I should say, if you hadn’t heard about this: there was a [report released by Anthropic](https://www.anthropic.com/threat-intelligence-report-september-2026) where they discussed that requests from users to Kimi models or models from DeepSeek were being rerouted to Claude. And some of these even included requests from, I think, a PLA [People’s Liberation Army] official, even in one instance. So really sensitive things that people thought they were using a Chinese model for, but was in fact being sent to Claude.

What I’d love to know is: what do you think the CCP officials who spoke to the CEOs of [Moonshot](https://www.moonshot.ai/) and DeepSeek about the data leaks to Claude, what do you think that conversation was about?

**Julian Gewirtz:** So the first thing I’d say is: I wonder at what level of technical sophistication that conversation happens, because there’s a version of that conversation — in our idealised version of, generally, globally, how governments and private sector should interact — that could be pretty technically sophisticated. But I think it’s fairly unlikely that that was the only kind of conversation that happened.

I think it’s more likely that there was a conversation about this — maybe that did occur at a technical level, or they sent in people from the [Cyberspace Administration](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cyberspace_Administration_of_China) or one of the real AI technical bodies that does exist to understand how this happened. But the political dimensions of that — the idea that it embarrassed China and embarrassed these companies — had to have been front and centre. And that’s the kind of thing that would probably happen somewhat distinct from the more technical conversation about what was actually revealed and how did that actually happen.

I think we all had the reaction reading the Anthropic report that, like, first, this is crazy. And it is a reminder of how the incredibly fast-moving Chinese efforts to catch up have led to a degree, in some areas, of sloppiness that is certainly not what a perfectly centrally planned version of an AI race from Beijing’s perspective would look like. And it is embarrassing. I mean, it’s deeply embarrassing for them.

And the broader point about [distillation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Knowledge_distillation) and dependence on American models, though: we were sort of talking just a second ago about some political dimensions of that conversation. It’s important to underscore that Beijing’s line on distillation is not, “It doesn’t happen, and how dare you.” It is precisely, actually, “This is normal practice –”

**Tom Reed:** Fair game. Yeah.

**Julian Gewirtz:** “– the United States is trying to twist this into something it’s not,” et cetera, et cetera.

And I was also quite struck that they connected that report to when Dario came out with the [call to pace the frontier](https://darioamodei.com/post/we-must-pace-the-frontier), and some of the China language there.

One of the core points I always make about China is that they connect dots in our system that we may not connect ourselves. And candidly, I think we do the same sometimes in their system; we can come back to that. But they connected, in very official, authoritative state media, that report that we were just talking about — including those really embarrassing disclosures — with the calls to pace the frontier, which included language about the need for the US to stay ahead of China. They said, “See, these are all part of the same initiative, the same effort to make Chinese AI look bad and keep the United States number one.”

And candidly, I don’t think too many people in the United States connected those. I’m not even sure that Anthropic necessarily meant them as part of some kind of coordinated thing. I don’t know. But they saw it that way, and it’s just a reminder of that core dynamic.

**Tom Reed:** Yeah, that makes sense.

### How do Chinese labs really view AI risk? [[00:23:18]](https://80000hours.org/podcast/episodes/julian-gewirtz-china-us-ai-deal/?t=1398)

**Tom Reed:** So it’s still deeply unclear how either the US government or the Chinese government might relate to a very rapid increase in AI capabilities. How do you think about the difference between how the American labs versus the Chinese AI labs think about AI risk?

**Julian Gewirtz:** It’s such an important question, because that distinction in each country between the governments and the labs is actually something that can sometimes get overlooked by either player. China often talks about the United States ecosystem as just one monolithic thing. Obviously, Americans often sometimes talk about the Chinese ecosystem in the same way.

And over the summer, my friend Dan Wang and I wrote an [essay in _The New York Times_](https://www.nytimes.com/2026/06/28/opinion/ai-race-china-us.html) that was arguing essentially that we needed to focus more on the competition for influence and bargaining and dynamics within the United States and China respectively than we do currently, where the focus is largely on the race between the two. And obviously that’s become pretty salient in the months since we wrote about that, which was right around the time of the [US government and Anthropic dispute](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anthropic%E2%80%93United_States_Department_of_Defense_dispute).

I guess what I would say there is, to my mind, the key difference is that the American labs — some of them, at least — have a demonstrated track record of taking safety somewhat seriously and doing certain things to disclose to the public, and to even in some cases constrain their own racing forward. I think it’s nowhere near what many of us would like to see, but there is something of a track record there. And candidly, we don’t have that on the Chinese side.

I think when people talk about these questions of where is the risk greater these days, the US government certainly doesn’t seem like it’s being particularly responsible. But I think there is reason to say that some of the American labs, at least, have behaved in a way that is a little bit more attuned to the safety concerns than some of the Chinese labs.

**Tom Reed:** Do you never entertain cynicism — like, cynicism toward the American labs? Like, you take this—

**Julian Gewirtz:** Do I? Absolutely.

**Julian Gewirtz:** The people who I find most interesting are largely not people I agree with. It’s not like I’m reading Chinese academics and nodding along saying, “Preach,” or whatever.

But for instance, there’s a guy named [Jiang Shigong](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jiang_Shigong) — and I can send you some stuff of his — but he is very far from somebody who I think shares any views with me, but I find him to be an enormously revealing analyst of contemporary China, of Xi Jinping. And he’s a very ambitious intellectual. He is very supportive of many of the things Xi Jinping does, and he’s definitely comfortably operating, by all accounts, in that system.

But when I think about who has been the most sort of precise framework generator that has helped me generate my own frameworks for understanding that system, his work is quite useful, and a bunch of it has been translated — even if I’m like, “I do not like the upshot of that for America.” But it’s important to actually reckon with those people.

And I would say, more generally, there is a set of government-aligned thinkers who are serious thinkers. These are not simply people who are doing propaganda work, but they are very supportive of what China is doing. And I think it’s actually really important for people in my position to read them, to reckon with them, to take their ideas seriously.

The best example of this, by the way, is Wang Huning, who we mentioned earlier, who’s one of Xi Jinping’s top advisers. He’s on the Politburo Standing Committee. He started off as [an international politics] professor at Fudan University, and a number of his early writings — all the way back from the 1980s and early 1990s — are still incredibly interesting, layered reads, and sometimes they get caricatured.

His most famous book is called _[America Against America](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/America\_Against\_America)_, and it sometimes is described as just an anti-America polemic. And there’s a lot of criticism of the United States in there, for sure, but there’s also all this really interesting language about how technologically advanced the United States is and how innovative the United States is. And when you think about how he has approached governing China, actually both sides of that are really important.

And a closer reading of that text — a closer understanding of this isn’t only the parts that are about what he sees in America and criticises, but also what he sees in America and envies — both of those impulses shape what he and Xi Jinping and other Chinese leaders have done. So yeah, it’s important to reckon with.

**Tom Reed:** What Chinese intellectual currents that are particularly relevant to AI policy do you think we should be aware of? So I’m vaguely familiar with the [Industrial Party](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Industrial_Party_(China)) as a movement. I’ve read [Lu Nanfeng and Wu Jing’s essay](https://www.readingthechinadream.com/lu-nanfeng-and-wu-jing-on-the-industrial-party.html) on this. Can you carve them into blocks that I should reckon with, or is that difficult to do?

**Julian Gewirtz:** So I’d say a couple things. First, there is a longstanding sort of futurist strand of writing in China. You mentioned earlier in our conversation the Alvin Toffler influence in the 1980s that I wrote about. And I think understanding these kind of techno-futurist visions in China, and the way in which they see industrial development and party leadership, is one really important strand of thinking.

A second, which used to be much buzzier a few years ago and has certainly diminished since then, is Chinese science fiction. [Jordan Schneider](https://www.chinatalk.media/about), who does the _[ChinaTalk](https://www.chinatalk.media/)_ podcast and is a friend, likes to talk about how influential sci-fi has been in shaping American and Western visions of the AGI future.

And there was this incredible flowering of science fiction writing in China over the course of the 1980s, 1990s, and 2000s. And it was one of those areas where you saw people doing politically sensitive writing, but somehow getting away with it under the sort of sci-fi banner. And I think it’s important for people who are trying to understand the kind of currents in China to look at that writing.

And obviously Liu Cixin is the most famous — _[The Three-Body Problem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Three-Body\_Problem\_(novel))_ is the most famous — but there are a range of others. There’s a guy named [Chen Qiufan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chen_Qiufan), who ended up actually [cowriting a book](https://www.ai2041.com/) with [Kai-Fu Lee](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kai-Fu_Lee) on AI futures, but is also just a really interesting sci-fi writer; a woman named [Hao Jingfang](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hao_Jingfang), who wrote an amazing sort of [novella](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Folding_Beijing) — long short story — about kind of inequality in Beijing. And so there’s a number of these things which are really interesting, even if the space for that writing is smaller now. But I think it reflects this kind of set of possibilities.

And then, I guess, third and finally, just to kind of foreground, is to say: reading these regime-aligned or regime-supportive intellectuals in China, who position AI at the absolute heart of the way in which power will be distributed in the future, and give that kind of deeper intellectual foundation to Xi Jinping saying something like “technology is the main battlefield of international competition” — that’s really important too, in addition to reading the people who are actually working on AI issues.

### Which AI model is the best China watcher? [[01:39:27]](https://80000hours.org/podcast/episodes/julian-gewirtz-china-us-ai-deal/?t=5967)

**Tom Reed:** And what about using the AI models themselves? Which AI model is the best China watcher?

**Julian Gewirtz:** Of the Chinese models?

**Tom Reed:** Across the whole range. If you’re doing research with a model, which one are you using? I’ve found, for instance, ChatGPT seems to be better at finding WeChat links than Claude, for whatever reason.

**Julian Gewirtz:** Yeah, it’s interesting you said that. I was about to say something similar, which is, I’m not terribly original on this, but yeah, I find for the kind of research that I’m doing — to the extent that I’m using AI to help me do it — ChatGPT somehow has seemingly greater facility with the Chinese parts of the internet than Claude. And I’ve heard some people say I should be checking out Gemini more on this front. I confess that I haven’t really. To the extent that I’m using this, I’m pretty satisfied with what I’m getting. But yeah, it is interesting.

And I will say, for me, what I have not done, but others have done — and there’s [some](https://academic.oup.com/pnasnexus/article/5/2/pgag013/8487339) really [interesting work](https://arstechnica.com/ai/2025/01/the-questions-the-chinese-government-doesnt-want-deepseek-ai-to-answer/) on this — is kind of comparing what you find when you research China on Chinese models and American models. Obviously we all know about certain censorship guardrails that are built in. It’s not surprising that you find much less about the Tiananmen crackdown on a Chinese model, but that, actually, because of the priority given to the training corpus being in Chinese, there are sometimes very different answers you get when you ask the question in Chinese versus in English — which is itself a really interesting thing, and I suspect is also probably true in some of the American models.

But that connection between the corpus that’s being used — the language of the corpus that’s being used to train — and the kind of epistemic consequences of that is something that I think is just going to become more and more important.

By the way, we are beginning to see a Chinese discourse on this too: people in China writing about the fact that what they choose to feed in is what others will be processing for centuries to come — and hoping to shape international discourse through shaping the kind of corpus of Chinese and China-relevant material — is a super interesting area that there’s some work happening on, and we need more.

**Tom Reed:** Do we have any idea what they’d be prioritising other than censorship? What narratives would they be actively trying to push?

**Julian Gewirtz:** Absolutely. So the simplest version is essentially propaganda, where the goal is to push a positive set of narratives about China and downplay criticisms of China; a positive set of narratives about Chinese leaders, downplay criticism of them. But then there’s a whole range of other topics, like Taiwan — where their goal is to maximally shape a version of understanding of Taiwan issues that comports with their official line.

And the idea that we could have models that would be unwittingly built in such a way that they reinforce that, I think, is the kind of concern that is really reasonable to have — particularly now that we begin to see corners of the sort of official and semi-official discourse in China talking about this as an opportunity for them.

### A world tour of China’s influence [[01:42:59]](https://80000hours.org/podcast/episodes/julian-gewirtz-china-us-ai-deal/?t=6179)

**Tom Reed:** A final question I have: where do you think are the best places on Earth to visit to understand China’s international strategy and its investment in the Global South?

**Julian Gewirtz:** I spent a bit of time when I was at the State Department working on this issue set and doing a lot of travel around it.

To focus on the Global South questions specifically, my own view is that it’s good to get a kind of spectrum of different places that have found different ways, and are finding different ways, of striking the balance between getting more benefit out of their ties with China and maintaining their own sovereignty and autonomy on the world stage.

So at one end of that spectrum you have India — a country that, because of the border conflict and other issues, decided to block a bunch of Chinese apps, and really try to push back against Chinese influence. And I think it’s super interesting and important to hear their perspective, which is not one-for-one with the Washington perspective, even though it is quite concerned about increasing Chinese influence.

Then I think Central Asia is a super interesting place, because of the dynamic of competition between China and Russia there. Obviously China and Russia are close strategic partners, but they also have some areas where they’re competing for influence, and Central Asia is one of them.

Another super interesting place, which I have not been to, but I think would love to sort of see and talk to people on this score, is Egypt — where Xi Jinping just went on a state visit — and the kind of question there of a country that has deep security ties with the United States, but is clearly making a major play to upgrade its relationship with China. Super interesting.

And then in the Western Hemisphere, I also think — whether it’s Mexico, where there has been a tonne of scale-up of Chinese companies manufacturing, or Peru, where China has been building this [megaport](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chancay_Port) on the Pacific coast — these are really significant stories.

And then finally, I would just say: every year, the first trip abroad that the Chinese foreign minister takes, for decades, has been to Africa. And it is a place where China, I think, has a much more complex and differentiated and layered strategy than some accounts would have you think. But whether you’re going to countries that have really gone all in and see the Chinese development model as something that they want to ride for their own development, or to countries that feel like they’ve gotten bad deals out of China but still know that they have to have a good relationship with Beijing — super worthwhile. I realise I have just essentially told you to go to every place in the world, but the upshot—

**Tom Reed:** I like an excuse to go everywhere.

**Julian Gewirtz:** Exactly, exactly. You should get the podcast to pay for it. But no, I guess to my mind, the upshot of all of that is: China has a global strategy. It is pursuing it in many different ways around the world. It wants global influence. It wants that influence to look different than American global influence has looked. But there’s no one place where you can go to see it all, because Beijing is doing so many different things in so many different places.

**Tom Reed:** Great. Well, it’s been a real pleasure, Julian. Thank you for coming on the show, and talk to you next time.

On March 23, 2003, a Patriot missile battery in northern Kuwait identified an incoming anti-radiation missile. The crew had just a few seconds to decide whether the threat was real. They fired before the ‘missile’ could get any closer — and killed both people aboard what turned out to be a British aircraft heading back towards friendly airspace.

The missile battery _did_ have humans in the loop, but the crew was working with a system that was right almost all the time, under time pressure that made it hard to assess the specifics. The Army’s own review found that crews had been trained to trust the system and given almost no basis on which to doubt it.

That was 2003 software, and the AI systems of today only make the problem harder. Today’s systems [can do far more](https://www.lawfaremedia.org/article/how-the-u.s.-military-learned-to-embrace-ai-warfare) than any technology in 2003 could, so the temptation to let them function more and more autonomously will continue to grow. As of 2026, [frontier AI companies are working with the US military](https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/5/1/pentagon-announces-deal-with-seven-ai-companies-for-classified-systems) on integrating AI tools. Many [experts](https://wtop.com/national/2026/05/as-the-pentagon-pushes-for-battlefield-ai-some-military-leaders-urge-caution/) are [worried](https://www.ungeneva.org/en/news-media/press-release/2026/08/renewed-call-united-nations-secretary-general-and-president) about what might happen if that integration isn’t done safely.

As the AI tools used by militaries become both more powerful and more autonomous, the scale of potential failure becomes increasingly large. Militaries already use autonomous fighter jets and drones. A growing share of intelligence analysis is based on AI, and cyberwarfare is [speeding up](https://www.anthropic.com/news/disrupting-AI-espionage) as AIs become more competent hackers.

Most people who want to work on risks from advanced AI don’t consider careers in national security. For some, this is a deliberate decision, because they don’t want to work in an industry that inherently includes violence and could cause significant harm to innocent people, or because they don’t support integrating AI into the military and don’t want to be involved in any way. We think both of these can be good reasons to choose other paths.

But we also think that some of the most dangerous uses of AI will arise in the context of national security, and that having people in security roles who are knowledgeable about risks from advanced AI could avert some of the worst possible AI outcomes. And because many people see national security work as a form of public service, and a chance to make their country and the world safer, we want to make it clear that we see a strong path to impact in this field. These roles aren’t for everyone, but if you’re a good fit, they are worth considering.

Note: this article is focused on national security roles within the United States. If you’re in a different country, some of the same logic applies, but we haven’t researched those roles.

## Why work on national security?

The AI safety case for national security work comes down to three things: the stakes of how AI is used, the shortage of safety-minded people working on reducing risks in this area, and the leverage that comes with the US government’s vast resources and the power it controls.

The work can also be personally fulfilling. Many people who work in national security chose it because they want to serve and defend their country. They often see the work as morally complex, but still good overall. This article is focused on AI risk, but patriotism is an additional reason for some people to consider this path.

### National security includes some of the most dangerous AI deployments

National security applications are among the most consequential — and potentially most dangerous — ways AI is being deployed. These include (but aren’t limited to) autonomous and semi-autonomous weapons, offensive and defensive cyber capabilities, intelligence analysis that feeds decisions about the use of force, and surveillance tools that could shift the balance of power between governments and their own citizens.

We’ve been living in a period with no major wars between global powers, and nuclear weapons haven’t been used since 1945. But we almost lost this relative peace a few times because of automated information processing systems. For instance, in 1983, when Lieutenant Colonel Stanislav Petrov saw that early detection systems were reporting five incoming US missiles, he was supposed to pass that information up the chain of command, which could have led to a Soviet strike on the United States in retaliation. Petrov took the time to think about it and reasoned that a real US strike would likely have involved hundreds of missiles, not five, and reported a system malfunction instead.

As AI systems become more [integrated](https://www.war.gov/Spotlights/Artificial-Intelligence/) into our [national security apparatus](https://www.brennancenter.org/our-work/research-reports/militarys-use-ai-explained), a modern-day Petrov would have a harder time making that call. Of course, today’s systems are smarter than those from the 1980s and less likely to make simple mistakes, but in some ways, that makes the problem even harder: if a very competent AI system says that it’s important to launch a counterstrike immediately, it may be hard for a human to question that recommendation and notice whether the AI made a mistake or is compromised or misaligned.

The sheer volume of AI-generated information may also make decision making more difficult than it was for Petrov: in September 2026, CNN reported that a source claimed an intelligence report generated using AI “[almost started a war](https://www.cnn.com/2026/09/18/politics/us-military-ai-false-intelligence-china-ship)” when it misidentified a Chinese ship’s cargo as containing components of a nuclear weapon. In this case, the mistake was identified before any serious harm was done, but as humans deal with increasing amounts of AI analysis, they’ll have a harder time digging into details to correct mistakes.

If AI systems are implemented within command and control, humans will likely end up with fewer opportunities to notice and stop an erroneous process before it leads to a catastrophic outcome. The systems we’ve developed have held up so far, and none of our mistakes have led to a global nuclear war. But if AI introduces new types of mistakes and new possible responses, this balance may become much less stable. There’s already more information available than humans can look at, so analysts will rely on automated processing to help them make sense of the data, making conclusions hard to verify, even if AIs aren’t making decisions independently.

Other AI capabilities could also become extremely dangerous in a national security context. AI systems are quickly developing superhuman hacking abilities, and hacks against critical systems could become increasingly common as powerful cyberwarfare tools become accessible to groups without much money or technical expertise. The same is true for biological weapons and other extremely dangerous technologies: it may become possible for relatively small-scale actors to launch attacks that only major powers could execute today.

To keep people safe as these technologies develop, we need people within the US national security apparatus who understand AI and are concerned about its possible risks. The US government has the resources and power to defend against these risks when they come from other actors, so it’s one of the best places in the world to work on stopping AI misuse and defending against some types of rogue AI behaviour. At the same time, the US security establishment is also using advanced AI models in new and potentially dangerous ways, so it’s important for the people within it to be knowledgeable about the risks and to work to make sure AI is used safely.

### National security needs more people who care about AI safety

The kind of person who worries the most about catastrophic risks from AI is rarely the kind of person who pictures themselves at the Department of War. People motivated by AI safety often cluster in research labs, academia, and a handful of policy organisations, which means the military, intelligence, and other agencies making some of the highest-stakes AI decisions can’t easily hire people with strong AI fluency and commitments to making AI go well. Although there are people focused on AI safety within many of these organisations, and there will likely be more as the issue becomes more mainstream, we still need many more talented people who care about AI safety working on national security.

### Government money shapes what AI companies build

Defense and national security account for an enormous share of US federal spending — roughly [half of the discretionary budget](https://fiscaldata.treasury.gov/americas-finance-guide/federal-spending/). And because the government spends so much money on defense, it has a huge amount of influence on corporate R&D. Procurement requirements, testing standards, and contract terms shape what AI companies build, what they’re allowed to deploy, and what safety practices become normal — often more directly than regulation does. The government’s role as AI’s largest and most demanding customer gives the people writing those requirements leverage over how the technology develops, including at the [frontier](https://www.war.gov/News/Releases/Release/Article/4475177/classified-networks-ai-agreements/) AI [companies](https://openai.com/index/our-agreement-with-the-department-of-war/) now seeking defense contracts.

In early 2026, when Anthropic and the US Department of War had a [public conflict](https://www.reuters.com/business/pentagon-clashes-with-anthropic-over-military-ai-use-2026-01-29/) over the licensing terms for military uses of Anthropic’s AI model, Claude, some of their central points of contention were [reportedly](https://www.bloomberg.com/news/articles/2026-02-16/pentagon-is-close-to-cutting-ties-with-anthropic-axios-says) about using Claude for fully autonomous weapons and for mass domestic surveillance. Anthropic wanted to bar the use of Claude for these activities; the Pentagon wanted to be able to use it for any lawful purpose. When Anthropic refused, the Pentagon designated it a “supply chain risk,” a label usually reserved for companies tied to foreign adversaries, and later came to an [agreement](https://www.nytimes.com/2026/02/27/technology/openai-agreement-pentagon-ai.html) with Anthropic’s competitor OpenAI. Few customers could have that kind of leverage over a company. That means whoever decides what the government asks for, including which safety features it requires or rejects, could have substantial influence over how this technology develops.

## Would you be a good fit?

There’s no single profile for careers in national security — the field includes intelligence analysts, programme managers, think tank researchers, and technical evaluators, and those jobs reward different strengths. But they share more than the job titles suggest: nearly all of them involve working inside large, hierarchical institutions, communicating across a technical / nontechnical divide, and earning trust in a culture that is often sceptical of new ideas and changes to established procedure.

### What skills are needed to succeed?

Most AI-relevant national security roles call for some combination of:

*   **Social and political skills:** National security institutions run on trust and informal networks even more than the rest of the government. Who you work with tends to matter more than your job title, so a relatively junior person whose mentor has an influential position may be able to achieve a lot. Compared to the tech industry, DC tends to be relatively traditional, so conventional professional norms (dress, behaviour) are important for many roles. But context matters a lot: roles that are more technical and are farther from elected officials may have more room for personal expression.
*   **Technical skills:** Some amount of technical skill is almost always helpful, but the degree of helpfulness varies — and you may need much less skill than you’d expect. If you’re used to the hiring standards at leading tech companies, it’s important to remember that your skills may go much further in organisations with few staff in technical roles. You don’t need to be able to build AI systems (with rare exceptions), but you’ll usually need to be comfortable reading and understanding a paper and explaining it to someone less technical than you are.
*   **‘Translating’ technical concepts for people with varied backgrounds:** In many roles, some of your most important work will involve helping technical and nontechnical people communicate, such as by helping an engineer understand what a policymaker needs and helping a policymaker understand how a system works. This means knowing enough to understand both sides of the conversation, and conveying information in simple language without slipping into condescension.
*   **Briefing:** This means being able to compress a detailed report or data set into a single page, or a few minutes of discussion. Decisions in this world are made by busy people, and the person who can summarise well shapes what gets understood.
*   **Writing:**[Policy writing](https://emergingtechpolicy.org/tips/policy-skills/#writing) is a different genre from academic writing: bottom line up front, short, and with clear action items. If you prefer to write long essays full of caveats and counterarguments, you might not enjoy writing in this style.

### What experience is useful?

People enter this work from many directions, but these are particularly useful:

*   **Military service:** A service record is useful for credibility and institutional knowledge, and many federal roles give preference to veterans. However, service isn’t required; most people in these roles don’t have it. Because AI progress is happening so fast and attaining high military rank can take many years, we don’t recommend that people enter the military with the goal of affecting AI policy, but if you already have military experience, it can certainly help.
*   **Graduate degrees:**[Policy master’s degrees](https://80000hours.org/career-reviews/us-policy-masters-degrees/) are particularly useful in DC, as are law degrees and PhDs in relevant fields.
*   **Intelligence or other government experience:** Time in any policy role builds networks and an understanding of how institutions work, and if you get a security clearance in the process, that opens up a much wider set of roles.
*   **Critical languages:** Knowing a language that’s relevant to key international AI safety issues is necessary for some roles and useful for many others. Mandarin and Russian are particularly helpful for some analysis and intelligence roles, although there are also many roles in these areas that don’t have any language requirements. For most people, it’s probably not worth spending a lot of time learning a language in order to work on AI safety within national security. But if you do have this background, it may help you.
*   **Legal fluency:** You don’t need a law degree, but it’s often helpful to feel comfortable reading statutes, regulations, and procedural documents. The culture tends to be conservative, and people often assume that statute or policy requires something to be done as it always has been. If you’re comfortable reading legal jargon and drawing your own conclusions, you may be able to help people find other options that they didn’t know would be allowed.

### What else do you need?

Beyond skills and experience, many national security roles come with practical requirements that are important to consider as you decide whether these roles could be a good fit for you:

*   For most government roles, you’ll need **US citizenship**. Most roles at think tanks and research organisations can be done by foreign nationals.
*   Many roles require a **security clearance**, and the process can be complicated and invasive. On the other hand, an active clearance compounds as a career asset: it makes you dramatically easier to hire for the most consequential roles. If this path appeals to you at all, it’s worth positioning yourself to start the process early — but keep in mind that clearances expire if they go unused for a few years. ([More on clearances from Emerging Tech Policy Careers.](https://emergingtechpolicy.org/tips/security-clearance/))
*   Some roles in the executive branch and most roles working for members of Congress effectively require **party affiliation**, and prior associations with one party (including donations) can lock you out of some roles under the other.
*   Most of these jobs require you to **live in or near DC**, or a regional hub for your agency. Remote work is limited, and often impossible for roles that require a security clearance.
*   Finally, you’ll need to **be comfortable with the basic premise of the work**. You don’t have to be enthusiastic about defense institutions, or think that the American military does only good things, but you do need to be comfortable working alongside the military. In addition, these are jobs serving the United States. If you see reducing AI risk as part of serving your country, this path could be a great fit. On the other hand, if it’s important to you to work in an environment that prioritises all of humanity equally, regardless of where they live, this path might not be the right fit for you, even if the impact case seems appealing.  
[](https://80000hours.org/career-reviews/national-security/)

## Downsides to working on national security

### Serious risk of doing harm

National security institutions are powerful, and their mistakes are hard to reverse. Working inside them could position you to prevent serious harm — or to contribute to it. You might do harm by:

*   Helping to build or legitimise dangerous capabilities that wouldn’t otherwise have been fielded, or fielded as quickly
*   Directly making a choice that contributes to a dangerous accident
*   Making harmful uses of AI more likely by allowing institutions to ‘safety-wash’ their dangerous AI deployments by pointing to supervision from safety experts like you
*   Entrenching AI systems in a way that makes it harder to stop using them later on, if they become dangerous in the future

The fact that so much of your work may be classified makes this problem worse. If you’re someone who usually talks difficult decisions through with friends or mentors, the level of required secrecy may make it hard to get enough perspective to notice if the work you’re doing is no longer addressing the problems you want to solve.

### Personal risks to you

Most of the roles discussed in this article involve sitting at a desk in the United States and never facing significant physical danger. But if you’re embarking on a career in national security, you should take into account that some of these roles (including technical roles in field intelligence) put people at risk of being injured or killed in the line of duty. In addition, some roles may expose you to personal harms like hacking attempts or other cyberattacks.

Beyond those dangers, working in national security exposes you to moral and psychological risks that are different from those in most other areas. For example, you may work closely with field operatives, who may be injured or killed as part of their duties. You may also face [moral injury](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Moral_injury) if you participate in projects that harm or kill other people, especially people who are not themselves dangerous. The secrecy required by many of these roles can make these risks harder to cope with, because you may not be able to process what you’re facing with the people in your life the way you would in most jobs.

### Risk of spending time on work that doesn’t matter

More prosaically, a lot of work in the national security establishment may simply not be very useful. These are large bureaucracies, and you won’t fully control what you work on. Projects can lose focus and become much less impactful than they initially seemed. It’s also common to spend a long time on a project that ends up getting cancelled, reorganised, or defunded, or to invest time and effort into building professional relationships that become irrelevant when a new administration comes in with new personnel and priorities.

### Long and opaque hiring process

The federal hiring process can often be slow and hard to predict. Because of civil service requirements, the hiring manager for a role is not always the person who actually decides who to hire, so it may be harder to straightforwardly use your resume and skills to get a job in the federal government than in most industries.

In addition, many national security–relevant roles require a [security clearance](https://emergingtechpolicy.org/tips/security-clearance/). Once you have one, you can often move into subsequent roles without repeating the whole process, so having a clearance is a useful asset for future roles; you can start working sooner if you have a clearance from a prior role. Because of this, some roles will heavily favour people who already hold an active security clearance, which can make getting into your first national security role harder.

For roles where you need to get a security clearance, the timeline isn’t up to you or the people you work with. For a Secret-level clearance, which is the most common level, an average case will take about 4–5 months, and a more complicated one can take 6–12 months. Top Secret clearances typically take about eight months, and cases with complicating factors could take more than a year.

If you fail a clearance application, you’ll have a harder time getting a clearance later. Because you can generally only be sponsored once a year, it’s better to avoid applying for a clearance unless you feel very confident you’ll pass. If your application looks likely to fail, you can sometimes withdraw it to avoid having a denial on your record, but it’s best not to rely on that option.

The form used in the clearance process asks, among other things, whether you have used any federally illegal drugs (including marijuana) in the past seven years. Answering “yes” will not necessarily disqualify you, but it can, and ongoing regular drug use likely will. It’s important to answer truthfully and fully. In most cases, not having used drugs in the past year is a mitigating factor, so don’t automatically screen yourself out of these roles if you have used drugs in the past. However, these roles probably won’t be a good fit if you regularly use marijuana or other federally illegal drugs and intend to continue doing so.

Because getting a clearance is such a long and involved process, several experts we talked to see it as a significant barrier to working on national security. It makes it harder to break into national security work for the first time, and it means that, if you do get a role, there will likely be at least four months before you can start working with classified information (although some roles will let you start earlier with limited information access). If your timelines are short or you’re eager to start working on important things soon, the clearance process may be a significant downside of these roles compared to other policy work.

### Lack of AI safety community

We think some of these roles may be especially valuable _because_ there aren’t many AI safety professionals doing this work. But the flip side is that you might be the only person in your department who is knowledgeable about the full range of risks from advanced AI; your colleagues might have negative opinions about the AI safety community, or not believe that the risks are actually plausible. You might find this lonely and demotivating, or find yourself drifting towards the opinions of the people around you and thinking less about AI safety over time.

### Lifestyle and expression constraints

Some of these roles — especially in the intelligence community — heavily restrict your actions and your freedom of expression. You might spend most or all of your workdays in a [SCIF](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sensitive_compartmented_information_facility) without your phone; anything you want to publish online will probably need review; you’ll have few chances, if any, to work remotely; you might even be asked to take regular polygraph tests.[1](https://80000hours.org/career-reviews/national-security/#fn-1) You might not even be able to tell important people in your life about your work. For more on this, see Emerging Tech Policy Careers’ page on the [downsides](https://emergingtechpolicy.org/institutions/executive-branch/intelligence-community/#downsides-to-ic-work) of intelligence work, some of which also apply to other national security roles.

## Top organisations

The institutional landscape of national security shifts constantly — offices are reorganised, programmes are renamed, and hiring rounds open and close unexpectedly when a new administration or budget takes hold. We’ve used this section to map some important agencies, but check their websites for updates if you plan to apply.

Note that this list doesn’t include roles limited to military officers or enlisted personnel. If your primary goal is to improve AI policy or safety, we think you’ll have better odds working outside the military, since most policy is made by civilians. However, if you’re already in the military, especially if you’re relatively high in the chain of command, that experience will likely be valuable to you in many national security roles, and laws giving preference to veterans may also help you get roles that might otherwise be inaccessible.

### Government

*   **[Department of War](https://www.war.gov/):** The largest AI adopter in government by far, spanning everything from the Chief Digital and Artificial Intelligence Office to individual service programmes. Requirements, testing, and acquisition decisions made here shape what gets built and used.
*   **[Department of Commerce](https://www.commerce.gov/):** Home to two very different offices that both matter enormously.
    *   **[Bureau of Industry and Security](https://www.bis.gov/):** Writes and enforces the export controls on AI chips — arguably the US government’s most consequential lever over frontier AI development, run by a strikingly small team.
    *   **[National Institute of Standards and Technology’s Center for Advancing Innovation and Standards for Super Intelligence](https://www.nist.gov/caissi):** Develops AI standards and evaluations and is one of the few places in the government doing technical work on frontier model capabilities.

*   **[Executive Office of the President](https://www.whitehouse.gov/eop/):** Coordinates AI and national security policy at the highest level, particularly through the National Security Council and Office of Science and Technology Policy. Realistically, you won’t get hired here early in your career; you’re more likely to be detailed or appointed to the Executive Office after building a track record elsewhere. These roles are likely to be very impactful if you can get them.
*   **[The intelligence community](https://www.intelligence.gov/):** This includes the CIA and NSA, as well as agencies that are less well known to the public, including the State Department’s Bureau of Intelligence and Research, the Defense Intelligence Agency, and the Office of the Director of National Intelligence, plus organisations like the Intelligence Advanced Research Projects Activity that fund frontier-relevant research. Many of these are analysis roles where AI fluency is scarce and valued, but they can have some of the highest lifestyle costs (see [downsides](https://80000hours.org/career-reviews/national-security/#downsides)).
*   **The enforcement side of government:** Often less discussed, but this is where controls become real. Agencies include the State Department’s [Directorate of Defense Trade Controls](https://www.pmddtc.state.gov/) (arms export licensing), the Treasury’s [Office of Foreign Assets Control](https://ofac.treasury.gov/) (sanctions), the Energy Department’s [National Nuclear Security Administration](https://www.energy.gov/nnsa) (nuclear security, with growing AI work), and the [Department of Justice](https://www.justice.gov/) and [FBI](https://www.fbi.gov/) (investigating violations). Rules that nobody enforces don’t constrain anyone, and these offices are chronically short of people with expertise in frontier AI.

### Think tanks

*   **[Center for Security and Emerging Technology](https://cset.georgetown.edu/):** A Georgetown University research centre that has become one of the most widely cited sources of data-driven analysis on AI and national security, including compute, the AI workforce, and US–China competition. Its work is read closely inside government, and several of its researchers have gone on to senior policy roles.
*   **[RAND Corporation](https://www.rand.org/):** One of the oldest defense research organisations in the US. It runs several federally funded research and development centres (FFRDCs) for the military, so its research often goes directly to the people making decisions. Its Center on AI, Security, and Technology focuses on national security risks from frontier AI.
*   **[Center for Strategic and International Studies](https://www.csis.org/):** A large DC think tank covering defense and foreign policy. Its Wadhwani AI Center works on AI policy, export controls, and US–China tech competition, and its reports and events are a common way for new ideas to reach policymakers.
*   **[Center for a New American Security](https://www.cnas.org/):** A defense-focused think tank with close ties to the national security establishment, and a steady flow of staff between it and senior Pentagon and White House roles. Its technology and national security programme covers military AI, AI safety and stability, and compute.
*   **[Special Competitive Studies Project](https://www.scsp.ai/):** Founded by former Google CEO Eric Schmidt to carry on the work of the National Security Commission on AI. It focuses on US technological competitiveness, especially against China. It puts more weight on winning that competition than on reducing risk, so its emphasis is different from most of the other organisations listed here.
*   **[Institute for AI Policy and Strategy](https://www.iaps.ai/):** A smaller, newer think tank focused on reducing risks from advanced AI. Its research covers compute and chip export controls, US–China dynamics, and the security of frontier AI systems.

### Research organisations

*   **[Centre for the Governance of AI](https://www.governance.ai/):** Conducts AI governance research, including research into threat modelling, military and geopolitical implications of AI, and AI adoption in the military (as well as other research areas that are not directly about national security).
*   **[Federation of American Scientists](https://fas.org/):** Science policy nonprofit that works on AI, emerging tech, and nuclear risk, and helps place technical experts in government.
*   **[Institute for Progress](https://ifp.org/):** Think tank focused on innovation policy, including research on AI security.

### FFRDCs and university-affiliated research centres (UARCs)

These centres do long-term research and analysis for government agencies. People who work at these organisations are often issued security clearances and therefore can have closer access to government decision making than independent think tanks. Note that all of these organisations do a wide variety of research, some of which is not relevant to AI safety and some of which may be actively harmful, so it’s important to find out the details of the individual project you are applying to work on — we would not recommend all jobs at these organisations. A few examples:

*   **[RAND](https://www.rand.org/):** Operates several FFRDCs for the Department of War and Department of Homeland Security, alongside its independent research.
*   **[MITRE](https://www.mitre.org/):** Nonprofit that runs FFRDCs across defense, cybersecurity, and civilian agencies, with a growing body of AI assurance and security work.
*   **[Department of Energy national labs](https://www.energy.gov/national-laboratories)** (e.g. Lawrence Livermore, Los Alamos, Sandia, and Oak Ridge): Home to some of the government’s largest computing resources; increasingly involved in AI for science and in evaluating frontier AI for national security risks.
*   **[Johns Hopkins Applied Physics Laboratory](https://www.jhuapl.edu/):** A UARC doing applied defense research, including on AI.

## Key roles to aim for

Because the national security landscape is so vast and changes so quickly, we aren’t listing specific roles. Instead, here are some tips that might help you decide how impactful a given job might be:

*   **Does the role help you build career capital?** Clearances, interagency experience, and a reputation for reliable technical judgement all compound. Especially early in your career, look for roles that leave you with at least one of these even if the specific programme fizzles.
*   **Who will you be working with?** Who you work with matters more than your job title. A relatively junior role near people making consequential decisions is often better than a senior-sounding role without the same connections, because you may have the opportunity to move with your boss if they get promoted.
*   **Does it touch the interagency process?** All else equal, roles where you engage with how decisions actually get made across agencies — drafting policy documents that circulate or staffing interagency working groups — tend to build more leverage and career capital than roles confined to one office’s internal work. However, there are many individual roles that are valuable despite a lack of engagement with interagency processes.
*   **Does this agency already have people who moved into national security or policy work mid-career?** If it has none or very few, that may be a sign that it’s less open to hiring those people, which may make it both a harder place to get hired and a harder place to have an impact on the most important AI problems.

## How to enter if you’re early career

Early in your career, your main goals are getting a foot in the door and building the credentials, such as a clearance and institutional experience, that open up more senior roles later. A few ways to get started:

*   **Apply for fellowships.** The [Horizon Fellowship](https://horizonpublicservice.org/), [TechCongress](https://www.techcongress.io/), and the [AAAS Science and Technology Policy Fellowships](https://www.aaas.org/programs/science-technology-policy-fellowships) all place people into government and policy roles, and they come with cohorts and networks that help you build connections and institutional knowledge.
*   **Start the clearance process early.** If this path appeals to you, look for a role where you can start the [clearance process](https://emergingtechpolicy.org/tips/security-clearance/).
*   **Start applying!** Many agencies have entry-level positions, and think tanks often hire research assistants and other people in junior roles.

## How to enter if you’re mid-career

Switching into government and policy roles mid-career can be difficult, because you may be too senior for most entry-level jobs to be a good use of your time, yet not have the policy experience to get a more senior role. National security roles in particular may rely on tacit knowledge and networks that many people build up over the course of their careers. These steps can help you make the switch:

*   **Apply for fellowships.** Policy fellowships can help people make this transition:
    *   The [Horizon Fellowship](https://horizonpublicservice.org/programs/become-a-fellow/) trains and places fully funded fellows at host organisations in emerging tech policy, including in national security positions.
    *   If you’ve started a career in academia, the [Belfer Technology and Geopolitics Fellowship](https://www.belfercenter.org/fellowship/technology-and-geopolitics) for pre- and postdoctoral candidates may be a good fit.
    *   The [US Tech Force](https://techforce.gov/) is a two-year programme for engineers to work in government, including as part of the [War Force](https://www.opm.gov/news/news-releases/war-force-to-recruit-top-engineers-to-enhance-american-military-technological-dominance/).

*   **Build your network and practise**[pitching yourself](https://emergingtechpolicy.org/tips/pitching-yourself-in-policy-contexts/). One of your challenges will be building a professional network that helps you get roles. It helps to have a clear answer to “What do you do?” that explains why your skills and background would be valuable outside the context you’ve worked in so far.
*   **Consider a nonpolicy role as a way in.** In some circumstances, taking a nonpolicy role can [help you break in](https://emergingtechpolicy.org/pathways/full-time-roles/#common-career-paths), but be wary of roles that don’t have a clear path towards the work you actually want to do.
*   **Use resources for a career switch.** If you’re coming from tech, the site [Tech to Gov](https://www.techtogov.org/) and [Public Interest Technology Resources](https://public-interest-tech.com/) both have helpful guidance and recommendations.
*   **Consider a graduate degree.** Graduate degrees can be particularly helpful for landing jobs in the federal government, both because they may provide knowledge and connections that will help in your work, and because federal hiring rules give preference to people with graduate degrees in some situations. If you’re thinking about getting a graduate degree for this purpose, a [policy master’s degree](https://80000hours.org/career-reviews/us-policy-masters-degrees/) may be worth considering.

## Next steps

### If you need to build career capital

*   **Begin [building your network](https://emergingtechpolicy.org/tips/networking/).** Many roles in this field are filled through networks and word of mouth. See our [networking advice](https://80000hours.org/career-guide/how-to-network/). It can also help to spend some time in DC if you can, and go to professional events to introduce yourself and talk to people working in areas that might interest you.
*   **Publish writing on relevant topics (including by starting a blog).** Writing some blog posts or publishing an article is a surprisingly good way to get known as someone with interesting and well-informed views on a topic.

*   **Build technical literacy and practise explaining things.** You don’t need to be a technical AI safety researcher, but for many roles, you do need to credibly demonstrate that you understand AI systems (technical degrees, work at AI companies, evaluations experience, and serious coursework all help). Many people coming from more technical communities find that the amount of technical background that ‘counts’ in DC is much less than they expect.

### If you want to learn more

#### Top recommendations

*   [Emerging Tech Policy Careers](https://emergingtechpolicy.org/): A free career resource website run by the Horizon Institute for Public Service. It covers pathways into policy, profiles of key institutions (including the [Department of War](https://emergingtechpolicy.org/institutions/executive-branch/department-of-defense/) and the [intelligence community](https://emergingtechpolicy.org/institutions/executive-branch/intelligence-community/)), and guides to specific policy areas (including AI, biosecurity, and cybersecurity). It’s aimed at people exploring or actively pursuing careers in tech policy, and is particularly useful for understanding how [different institutions](https://emergingtechpolicy.org/institutions/) work, where you might [fit](https://emergingtechpolicy.org/essentials/policy-fit-testing/), and what you might want to [read next](https://emergingtechpolicy.org/areas/ai-policy/).
*   [How AI could transform the nature of war](https://80000hours.org/podcast/episodes/paul-scharre-ai-warfare-autonomous-weapons/): Paul Scharre, a former Army Ranger who led the Pentagon team that wrote the US military’s first policy on autonomous weapons, discusses how AI could change warfare and what happens when military decisions start moving faster than humans can follow.

#### Further recommendations

*   Career review: [AI policy in the US government](https://80000hours.org/career-reviews/ai-policy-us-government/)
*   Career review: [Technical governance](https://80000hours.org/career-reviews/technical-governance/)
*   Career review: [AI security](https://80000hours.org/career-reviews/ai-security/)
*   Podcast: [Helen Toner on the geopolitics of AI in China and the Middle East](https://80000hours.org/podcast/episodes/helen-toner-ai-policy-washington-dc/)
*   Podcast: [Sam Winter-Levy and Nikita Lalwani on how AI won’t end nuclear deterrence (probably)](https://80000hours.org/podcast/episodes/sam-winter-levy-nikita-lalwani-ai-nuclear-deterrence/)
*   Podcast: [Jake Sullivan on Navigating AI Uncertainty and Managing Competition with China](https://www.cognitiverevolution.ai/jake-sullivan-on-navigating-ai-uncertainty-and-managing-competition-with-china-2/) (on _The Cognitive Revolution_)

### Speak with us

If you think this path might be a great option for you, but you need help deciding or thinking about what to do next, our team might be able to help.

We can help you compare options, make connections, and possibly even help you find jobs or funding opportunities.
