title: Dancing with the trophy shortage
content:
It’s easy to get distracted by (and hooked on) the quest for a trophy. It’s easy to measure and a bright light to focus on.

But this skips the key question: _What’s it for?_

The Savannah Bananas never won their league. But they made more money (and their fans had more fun) than any other team.

Your favorite episode of the [Mel Robbins](https://youtu.be/cWZI2RyI9wM?si=npzbEXY6YOdx_63q) show might not be the one that got the most views. And of course, the best video on YouTube is unlikely to be the one that went the most viral. That’s simply the easiest to measure.

High school sports seems to be about solving the trophy shortage, but is that what it should be for? Are all the other teams and all their athletes failures? Or is it simply a shortcut that lets the coach off the hook when they hesitate to do the hard work of developing their students?

If it’s easy to measure, it might not be the thing you ought to be measuring. In fact, it probably isn’t.

title: Bing Gordon: Learning From Bezos, Jobs, and Spielberg
content:
[The Knowledge Project Podcast](https://fs.blog/knowledge-project-podcast/)

Bing Gordon is the former Chief Creative Officer of Electronic Arts and a partner at Kleiner Perkins.

He served on Amazon’s board for more than a decade, a seat he earned after giving Jeff Bezos five ideas. The first was Amazon Prime. Bing describes the week two directors told him they wanted to resign, and the fix he proposed: Bezos opens each meeting with what’s on his mind, and six-page memos replace slide decks.

He explains Bezos’s first rule for the board, “first, do no harm,” and the “institutional no” Bezos wanted the board to help Amazon avoid. He lays out the three behaviors Bezos looks for in people who are right a lot, why Bezos dropped one-on-ones, and how every Amazon candidate faces a seven-person interview loop built on the leadership principles.

Bing then turns to what games taught him. He explains why moving a game from an 80 to a 90 doubles sales, why Steven Spielberg recut films until nobody left their seat, and how expansion packs for The Sims shaped his pitch for Prime.

He shares the David Ogilvy lessons that never made the books, including that 90% of people who recall an ad remember the headline and only 25% remember the body copy.

title: Science After Super Intelligence
content:
_And even when the external world has granted all it can, there still remain the searchings of the mind and the longings of the heart._

—Arthur C. Clarke, _Childhood's End_, 1953

As the world attempts to bring artificial intelligence into focus, it is hard to think of a modern scientific project with a wider range of implications for the future. Some hold that AI has already reached its [maximum capabilities](https://nautil.us/deep-learning-is-hitting-a-wall-238440), while others maintain that we stand at the beginning of an [exponentially expanding demigod](https://www.ft.com/content/03895dc4-a3b7-481e-95cc-336a524f2ac2), a singularity, the point beyond which it will be impossible for humans to comprehend the accelerating insights of a “super intelligence.”

If the more radical proposition holds, that a singularity is afoot, then the assumption is that everything we do, and even things we cannot dream of, will soon be done by machines. For science, this means that the utilitarian problems we seek to solve will be solved at ever faster rates by machines. What does this mean for scientists? Will there be anything left to do, or are scientists out of jobs?

**Read more:**[**“The Thrill of Science in 2042”**](https://nautil.us/the-thrill-of-science-in-2042-1270684)

Astrobiologists must confront a similar thought that is discouraging for people who have dedicated their lives to discovery: What if an alien civilization somewhere out there has already come to know all the mysteries we hope to discover? More poignantly, what if such a species landed on our planet with all of their knowledge in hand (or in tentacle, or in ever-shifting amorphous goo)?

Well, there would be quite a lot of work to do. Communication with such a creature would be a challenge in itself. After that, considerable effort would be required to learn what they know. Such learning might proceed in stages and might take generations. There might be types of knowledge that do not overlap with ours for cultural and philosophical reasons, and we would [need to debate](https://www.science.org/doi/10.1126/science.ado7069) the meaning of such differences with ourselves and perhaps with them. Our lives would be anything but boring, and the amount of interesting work to do might even expand.

Many AI researchers think that such an alien is about to land on, or rather grow out of, our planet. An intelligence that is alien both by virtue of the vastness of its knowledge base and the incomprehensibility of its solutions. Many assume that such a creature will rapidly eliminate the need for scientists, but this presumption focuses only on the utilitarian aspects of science—the idea that science is about producing solutions that are useful to society, typically expressed in economic terms.

Indeed, science triumphed in its utility as it contributed to medicine, a greater abundance of crops, aerospace transportation, digital computers, the internet, magnetic resonance imaging, and, perhaps, large language models. All perfectly adhering to the “[Endless Frontier](https://nsf-gov-resources.nsf.gov/2023-04/EndlessFrontier75th_w.pdf)” predicted in postwar America. Utilitarianism is a good reason to invest in science, but it is shaky ground for a deep philosophy about the meaning of science. Technology is largely about optimizing on a task, science seeks something deeper, and this is often the pursuit of understanding, whose long-term benefits are impossible to predict. Even with tools in hand, such as AI, our focus should be on the challenge and meaning of engaging in tool-assisted activities as human beings. Consider the board games chess and Go, the marathon, and the mechanical watch.

In 1997, Deep Blue played, and beat, Garry Kasparov, widely considered one of the greatest players the game has known. In 2016, [AlphaGo defeated Lee Sedol](https://nautil.us/playing-go-with-darwin-238069), the strongest Go player the world had ever seen. By 2017, AlphaZero had taught itself in nine hours to play chess at a level no human will ever match. The outcome was not the collapse of chess. On the contrary, more people play chess now than at any point in its history. Chess.com surpassed 150 million members in the post-AlphaZero era, and over-the-board tournament participation has grown in parallel. Top grandmasters now study with game engines, and tellingly, the engines have become coaches rather than replacements. The grandmaster’s relationship with the chess engine sharpened the grandmaster’s game, rather than retire the player. The moves played in human tournaments are the player’s own, and the game’s meaning is that of the players, not of the silicon that has long since outclassed them.

The fastest car in the world, the Bugatti Chiron, can complete the 26.2 miles of a marathon in around 12 minutes. Near-superhuman world record holder Sebastian Sawe, who completed the London Marathon in 1 hour, 59 minutes, and 30 seconds, is ten times slower than the car. No one watching Sawe would conclude that the car is faster than humans. The marathon was never a means of transport. It is a challenge to the body, and the physiological question is, how far can we push the flesh before it fails?

Seiko introduced the first quartz watch in 1969. The Seiko Astron was accurate to within a few seconds per month, far more accurate than any mechanical watch of the time. The mechanical watch was on the verge of extinction, and the Swiss watch industry was decimated by the so-called “quartz crisis” of the 1970s. However, the industry survived and flourished by creating ever more complex and ingenious mechanical timepieces. The tourbillon, for example, was invented in 1795 to compensate for gravity in pocket watches. Today, there are many wristwatches with a tourbillon that serve no purpose other than to demonstrate the skills of the watchmaker.

The pattern discernible across these three examples is a transition from the belief that utility is the unique metric of progress to the deeper understanding that what we care about is craft and meaning. The utility of the activity might have been an original focus, but people came to realize that what they more profoundly cared about was the craft, style, and meaning of the activity. And mastering the activity was measured against the tradition in which one was practicing. And from this constellation of craft, style, and meaning derives the very practical principles of curiosity, search, and abduction, from which truly novel discovery derives.

And similar epistemic disruption has already occurred in history. The separation of natural philosophy into natural science and philosophy, which can be compared with the breakup of the Beatles, the forced exile of Romeo from Verona, or the disintegration of the 1997–98 Chicago Bulls.

Scientists might say that we no longer need to be mystified by matter, as we can measure it, we can have theories about it, and we can even make predictions about it. Yet philosophers are not deterred by this progress, many new details and measurements which science has provided, have opened new territory for philosophy, making the philosophical problems of the nature of matter and the universe more expansive. Thus, for example, the strangeness of quantum mechanics led to so many deep philosophical questions that the physicists started to tell each other to “shut up and calculate” and to stop worrying about the strangeness of the quantum world and instead to use the mathematical tools of quantum mechanics. But the philosophers, of course, have continued to ponder over the problems of quantum mechanics, to the point of making quantum foundations an important part of fundamental physics.

If AI were to reach the singularity, and solve hard problem after hard problem exponentially, then we would be left to explore the frontiers of our most immediate problems and be astrobiologists post-contact or philosophers’ post-science. Humans would be trying to make sense of other humans, and the rest of life in the universe. After all, early Western scientists saw their task as understanding the mind of God, and they were not discouraged by the assumption that something supernatural already knew the answers to their questions. If anything, the belief in a designer gave them hope that there were rules to be uncovered. If AI were to go singular, it would do so at a rate that we cannot keep up with, and in a language that we do not, or cannot, understand. As our colleague Ted Chiang has [observed](https://www.nature.com/articles/35014679), we may face a world of hermeneutics, in which we are constantly trying to decipher AI’s progress, communications, and actions.

As science changes, so too must our understanding of how to do it. The watchmaker’s case of the quartz movement which, by making accurate timekeeping so cheap and so universal, forced the mechanical watch into more elaborate and creative products of human hand and ingenuity, suggests that as science is relieved of the burden of the next predictive equation or of the next molecular structure, it can turn its attention to what science has always done underneath the surface of these things—namely to ask what on earth do these things mean?

Perhaps the most impressive example of how the pursuit of understanding can be successful is the history of neural networks themselves. Frank Rosenblatt, an American psychologist, was one of the pioneers of neural networks. In 1958, he described how a machine could learn by adjusting the weights of its connections in the same way as the brain adjusts the synapses between its neurons. However, in 1969, Marvin Minsky and Seymour Papert wrote the book _Perceptrons_ in which they described neural networks as an interesting object of scientific study but a sterile direction of applied research into intelligence. For these and other reasons in the 1970s, neural networks fell out of favor in computer science, a so-called “AI winter."

Geoffrey Hinton, who won the 2024 Nobel Prize in Physics for his work on neural networks, was discouraged by his PhD supervisor from working with them, suggesting that it would be a waste of time and effort. Hinton persevered under the belief that intelligence machines should learn bottom-up from the record of human behavior, and not top-down from definitions and abstractions of analytical reasoning. The project has been so successful that Hinton has become one of the [most outspoken proponents of AI safety](https://nautil.us/ai-engineers-are-having-their-oppenheimer-destroyer-of-worlds-moment-1284956) arguing for the regulation and slow-down of AI research.

In a further twist, much recent progress in AI has been driven by the application of GPUS (Graphic Processing Units) and TPUS (Tensor Processing Units) to training new Deep Neural Network architectures, neither of which were originally developed for AI application. GPUS were designed to solve the problems of real-time 3D graphics rendering in computer games, and TPUS are derived from Systolic Array technology invented to minimize memory bottlenecks in parallel computing. The application of these technologies to AI required an understanding that what all these problems had in common was the need for large matrix multiplications. The mathematical field of linear algebra, with its unifying concepts, is the glue connecting entertainment to edification.

The science of AI itself needs rethinking. If psychology had a replication crisis of some sort, where separate labs failed to replicate results, we face a replication catastrophe in AI research. Most methods are custom one-offs, applied to ever-changing, mostly proprietary models, part of a huge zoo of possibilities. Most studies are unconnected ephemera, disappearing in a distributed landscape. We need to make meaning, not only among machines, but of machines. It is still an open question how fully we can [translate between different intelligences](https://nautil.us/ai-could-help-humans-understand-animals-1211108), even in a world without gods. It remains to be seen how well we can even understand [what it is like to be a bat](https://www.sas.upenn.edu/~cavitch/pdf-library/Nagel_Bat.pdf). Meaning making remains a human endeavor, even if some new intelligent species provides us with things and solves problems for us.

Whether the AI we have is all we get, or whether we come to inhabit a post-singularity world, there will be much to do. Thinkers of all types are needed now more than ever. At the very least, an individual must make meaning from new machine assisted discoveries: It is one thing to discover a new behavioral or pharmacological intervention, and altogether another challenge to verify, test for safety, educate, and diffuse the discovery into a complex society. It is of even greater importance to discuss, contextualize, and philosophize new discoveries, all activities without end. Perhaps we are back to the Greek ideal of _eudaimonia_ —living among gods while living meaningful lives. The marathoner does not stop running because the car is faster, she runs because the running was always the point. ![Image 1](https://lede-admin.nautil.us/wp-content/uploads/sites/70/sites/3/nautilus/nautilus-favicon-14.png?fm=png)

title: The Everlasting Life of Maxwell’s Demon
content:
James Clerk Maxwell had good reason to feel contented in 1867. That year the Scottish physicist explained how the properties of gases derive from the frenetic motions of their inscrutable molecular particles. Two years earlier he had published a theory that united electricity and magnetism, one of the supreme achievements of 19th-century science, and a foundational law of physics. Maxwell had even made the first-ever proper color photograph. He was arguably the most distinguished physical scientist in Great Britain. But something deep in the laws of physics was troubling him. To get around it, Maxwell enlisted the help of a demon.

The problem was the second law of thermodynamics. It was inferred in the mid-19th century by the German physicist Rudolf Clausius. In Clausius’s formulation, the second law insisted that heat can never spontaneously pass from a cold substance to a hotter one. This is what we know intuitively: Hot coffee always cools, but cold coffee never spontaneously gets hot again.

This story is from “The Hot Issue,” the latest from _Nautilus_.  
To get it in print, **[join by Nov 30](https://nautil.us/hotissue?utm_source=beehiiv&utm_medium=email&utm_campaign=issuerelease-issue69-t1-202611&utm_term=free)**.

Clausius’ contemporaries were alarmed by what his second law implies. If heat is always passing from hot to cold, this means that all concentrations of heat are gradually dissipated and become a uniform thermal buzz in the background: Everything ends up at the same temperature. There must come a time when this is all there is. All pockets of energy will be dissipated, and no further change of any consequence can happen. The Scottish-Irish scientist William Thomson (later made Lord Kelvin) called this the heat death of the universe—not, as the name might imply, an infernal conflagration, but on the contrary an anticlimactic running down of everything.

The dreary end of all things may be a long way off, but for a devout Christian like Maxwell, the remoteness was no consolation. He believed in the eternal life promised by the scriptures. But he was also too much the scientist to accept that Christian doctrine could conflict with physical laws. And what about human free will, the means by which individuals could seek salvation? What could that mean in a world enslaved by the second law?

Theories in physiology then made the world and human behavior seem deterministic and inevitable, says historian of science Matthew Stanley of New York University, author of _Huxley’s Church and Maxwell’s Demon_. Maxwell, says Stanley, “was trying to figure out how there could be a ‘hole’ in theories that allowed for free will without giving up on laws of physics.” Stanley points out there was no great schism between theistic scientists like Maxwell and naturalists who saw no need for God’s involvement in the running of the universe. Both believed in natural laws like the second law and Isaac Newton’s laws of motion, and devout believers tended to feel sure these could be reconciled with an omnipotent God.

In 1867, Maxwell set about looking for a loophole that might safeguard his faith. He wrote to his friend Peter Guthrie Tait, who was preparing a book on thermo-dynamics, to say that he believed he had found one. In the “kinetic theory of gases” that Maxwell had just developed, the properties of gases—such as the fact that their pressure is proportional to their temperature—could be understood within a “microscopic” picture that considered the motions of the component molecules.

In this view, hotter gases have higher-energy and faster molecules on average than colder ones—but there is always a statistical spread of energies. If, Maxwell argued, you could measure the number of molecules with different energies in a gas at any given temperature, the graph would look like a sort of bell curve. If we raise the temperature of the gas, the peak of the bell curve shifts to higher energies, but also the hump itself flattens and broadens.

This, at any rate, is how things would look for a gas with an equal temperature everywhere—a gas at thermal equilibrium. But there’s not a lot you can do with a gas like that. If, on the other hand, you have a gas that is hotter in one region than another—if it’s out of equilibrium—you can extract useful work from it. The hotter region will have a higher pressure, and so it could push a piston into the colder region, driving some kind of engine. That was the basis of the steam engines of the Industrial Revolution, which had prompted the invention of the science of thermo-dynamics to predict and hopefully improve the efficiency of such devices.

But there is a bitter truth to the second law: It works to smooth away any such useful differences in temperature. In a gas with a hot region, the more energetic molecules will inevitably get spread out among the less energetic ones until energy is, on average, spread evenly. It’s just like stirring the cream in your coffee: The two will inevitably mix.

Once that has happened, there’s no going back. You can’t unstir the coffee. There is no physical law which says that the reverse is impossible—the chance that all the hotter molecules in a room might, just by chance, congregate in a hot cluster in one corner is not zero. But the chances of that happening are so astronomically small that it might as well be.

To defeat the second law, Maxwell needed to find some way of marshaling gas molecules so that the normal tendency for hot and cold regions to equalize would be reversed. If you could arrange for that, you could harness the temperature difference to do useful work. For this seemingly miraculous feat, the Christian physicist summoned a demon.

In truth, Maxwell himself never called it that. Heaven forbid! In his letter to Tait, he merely postulated a “finite being”—an “intelligent being endowed with free will”—small enough to “see” each molecule of the gas and able to keep track of it. When Thomson later mischievously dubbed this entity a demon, Maxwell grumbled to Tait: “Call him no more a demon but a valve.”

Why a valve? Because the demon’s job was to separate the hot molecules in a gas from the cooler ones by controlling their passage across a dividing wall between two compartments, using a trapdoor (assumed to be frictionless so that it takes essentially no energy to operate it). Whenever the demon sees a hot, fast-moving molecule coming toward the trapdoor from the left (say), it opens the door to let the molecule through. Whenever a cooler, low-speed molecule approaches from the right, the demon does likewise.

Gradually the demon segregates the hot and the cool molecules into the two compartments. From a gas with an initially uniform temperature on average, it creates one with a temperature difference—which can then be used to do work, such as pushing a piston. In fact, what the demon is using to reverse the second law is the _information_ it collects about the gas molecules. It follows “that the dissipation of energy depends on the extent of our knowledge,” Maxwell wrote in his 1872 book _Theory of Heat_.

Maxwell’s theory seemed to some of his fellow Christians to justify belief in eternal life. In 1875, Tait published a book with fellow physicist Balfour Stewart titled _The Unseen Universe_, in which they argued that the immortality of the soul can be consistent with the laws of physics, thanks to the ability of providential beings with the abilities of Maxwell’s demon. These, Tait and Stewart wrote, “restore energy in the present universe without spending work,” and act as God’s agents of everlasting life after death.

The existence of a providential being, however, probably overstepped Maxwell’s intent. “I don’t have any reason to think that Maxwell was suggesting something like the demon actually existed,” Stanley says.

Nevertheless, the demon threw down a gauntlet to scientists to prove why it couldn’t exist, spurring generations of important insights into physics. “I feel like every generation of physicists feels the need to slay Maxwell’s demon again, with the best theories of their time,” says Stanley. “The fact that it keeps coming back suggests something about it remains persuasive.”

As the 20th century unfolded, breaking the second law might still have been good for the tenets of Christianity, but it was becoming a cardinal sin in science.

In 1929, the Hungarian physicist Leo Szilard, a friend of Einstein’s, reformulated Maxwell’s demon in search of an answer. Szilard reimagined the demon as a kind of machine—not unlike the refrigerator that he and Einstein designed and patented the following year. (Fridges appear to reverse the flow of heat from hot to cold, but only at the cost of consuming energy and dissipating some of it as heat.) Szilard thought the flaw lay in the energy the demon expended in collecting information about the molecules by measuring their speed. But it’s not obvious that this need be a problem in principle, since there’s no obvious limit to how small we can make that energy.

Scientists had also begun to wonder whether life itself works as a kind of Maxwell’s demon. After all, don’t living organisms seem to achieve something comparable?

Another way of stating the second law is in terms of changes in the quantity called entropy, which, loosely speaking, might be considered a measure of disorder. According to the second law, the total entropy of the universe must increase in every process of change. But for as long as living organisms remain alive, they maintain organization in the face of such entropic decay. Although they “pay” for this order by consuming energy and dissipating heat into their surroundings, increasing entropy overall, still this ability of life to resist the second law with their own boundaries seemed puzzling.

In 1924, the physiologist Archibald Hill, who won a Nobel Prize two years earlier for his work on how muscles produce work and heat, wondered whether living cells might, like the demon, “be able to sort molecules [and] to use the energy of the more rapidly moving”; in effect, mining their environment for heat, a molecule at a time. The Irish chemist Frederick Donnan agreed, saying that at the tiny scales of biological cells and molecules, the second law might not be binding.

It was a tempting idea, but scientists proved it doesn’t work. Biology does, at the molecular scale, seem to achieve things that run counter to what we’d naively expect: to pump ions and molecules in an “uphill” direction to make them more concentrated, say. But such processes, like fridges, consume energy, apparently undermining the second law in one region only by observing it overall. By the mid-20th century, scientists realized there were no real Maxwell’s demons that could undermine the second law.

Why not? The reason turned out to be subtle. In 1961, the German-American physicist Rolf Landauer, working at IBM’s research laboratory in Yorktown Heights, began thinking about Maxwell’s thought experiment from the perspective of the information theory devised in the 1940s by telephone engineer Claude Shannon to explain how information can be most efficiently encoded and transmitted in telecommunications.

The demon can, from this perspective, be thought of as carrying out a kind of computation: It gathers input data (about the molecules’ movements) and works out, based on that information, whether to perform an action (open the trapdoor). Landauer showed that any computation can in principle be done with zero energy consumption and dissipation, so long as it is fully reversible. This entails storing every bit of information involved in the calculation—all the 1s and 0s on a digital computer.

Landauer showed that if, on the other hand, all these bit values are erased—setting them all to zero, say, and thus throwing away the information they stored—then each bit of lost information has an unavoidable cost in energy dissipation and a corresponding boost in the total entropy.

So, here’s the problem for the demon: As a “finite being,” it has a finite brain. At some point, it can’t accumulate more information about the gas without freeing up memory by throwing away previous information: in other words, by forgetting. The reason Maxwell’s demon can’t undermine the second law in the long run is not because of any energy needed to collect the information and work the trapdoor, but because it must eventually forget information—and that costs entropy.

All the same, until it needs to wipe its memory, the demon can seem to be beating the second law, capturing energy from random molecular chaos and using it to do work, purely thanks to its information-gathering.

Today, then, we understand that Maxwell’s argument reveals a deep connection between energy and information. It suggests that knowledge itself can be harnessed as a kind of fuel, while pointing to fundamental limits in the energy efficiency of computation (a literally burning issue now that we are confronted with energy-voracious data centers feeding AI). The second law remains intact, but Maxwell’s argument shows how to put it to new uses.

In 2010, a team of physicists at the University of Tokyo, led by Shoichi Toyabe, reported a striking demonstration of that, by interconverting work and information experimentally. They could shunt a tiny polystyrene bead barely 300 nanometers across systematically in a particular direction, doing useful work, by taking advantage of the information they gathered about the bead’s position.

The researchers placed the bead in a fluid between two glass plates and tethered the bead to the upper plate using a polymer molecule. Left to its own devices, the bead jiggled around randomly in the fluid. The team used electrodes on the lower plate to create a kind of energy staircase for the bead so that, if it circulated in one direction it hopped between ever “higher” (greater energy) steps, whereas in the other direction it hopped to lower steps. These hops happened at random because of the thermal motion, but on average they moved the bead down the staircase because it will tend to head toward a lower energy, like water flowing downhill.

Now the physicists took on the role of the demon. They measured the bead’s position using a microscope and then applied an electrical barrier that acted like a trapdoor to prevent the bead from moving to lower steps. If the bead happened randomly to jump up a step, the barrier was moved to stop it subsequently tumbling back down. By taking advantage of information gathered about the bead’s position, the physicists forced the bead to move steadily uphill and gain energy. Although the whole experiment consumed and dissipated energy overall, nothing but random thermal jiggling, along with the information that informed the positioning of the barrier, drove the uphill motion. In other words, the team had converted information about the bead into energy.

A quantum version of Maxwell’s demon introduces a new wrinkle, because the rules of quantum mechanics make it possible to do things with information that are impossible with classical physics. Two quantum particles can be prepared in a so-called entangled state, meaning that their properties are interdependent and correlated. If one quantum bit, for example, is measured to have a value 1, the other of the entangled pair must be 0. They are said to share _mutual information_, so that we can find out about one particle by looking only at the other.

In 2008, physicist Hossein Partovi of California State University, Sacramento, showed how entanglement can be used to reverse the spontaneous flow of heat from a hot object to a cold one. That might seem to violate the second law, but in fact it reveals that the _classical_ second law of regular thermodynamics is only an approximation to the full _quantum_ second law that allows for the effects of mutual information in entanglement. In the latter case, the entanglement itself functions as a sort of fuel that can drive a reverse flow of heat, creating a sort of refrigeration that might be useful in devices like quantum computers. But again, it doesn’t come free. As the flow proceeds, the entanglement gets used up and destroyed, so that the quantum second law remains intact.

Today, we are still coming to grips with the implications of Maxwell’s pesky demon. There are profound implications of the fact that we can perform work simply by knowing about the fine details of the molecular world, that a thermodynamics of ignorance and forgetting exists. These things point to fundamental limits on the energy efficiency of manipulating information, whether that’s in computers or in our brains. And they help us to understand how life sustains itself in the face of entropic demands.

Whether they rescue the Christian faith from a conflict with physical law, as Maxwell hoped, is another matter. Yet, says Stanley, religion did not disappear from science because it was considered inconsistent with it. It was simply that they spoke to different concerns. Seen that way, Maxwell’s demon was one of the last ideas that bridged the two worlds. It was, Stanley says, “a thought experiment that was useful both for religion and science.” ![Image 1](https://lede-admin.nautil.us/wp-content/uploads/sites/70/sites/3/nautilus/nautilus-favicon-14.png?fm=png)

title: For the First Time, This Dazzling San Francisco Snake is Being Released Into the Wild
content:
The distinctive-looking San Francisco garter snake (_Thamnophis sirtalis tetrataenia_) lives a perilous existence. Only a few thousand remain across San Mateo and Santa Cruz, and the species has been on the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service’s endangered list since 1967 (the year the list originated).

But there’s new hope for the long-term survival of the species after 62 snakes were released into the wild from the San Francisco Zoo. It’s the first time that San Francisco garter snakes bred in captivity have been placed back into their natural habitat. The hope is that the reptiles will become self-sustaining.

**Read more: “**[**This Snake’s Tail Has a Fake ‘Spider’ at the Tip**](https://nautil.us/this-snakes-tail-has-a-fake-spider-at-the-tip-1284917)**”**

The approach is known as head-starting, where animals are born in a zoo or another managed conservation environment, protected when they’re at their most vulnerable stages of development, and then rewilded at an early age. Experts were strategic at picking the spots in San Francisco most in need of a fresh influx of young garter snakes, both in terms of population numbers and genetic diversity.

“This is an extraordinary accomplishment for everyone who has worked for generations to protect this remarkable species,” biologist Karine Tokatlian, from the Midpeninsula Regional Open Space District, said in a [statement](https://www.sfzoo.org/a-new-generation-of-san-francisco-garter-snakes-returns-to-the-wild/). “Seeing these young snakes returning to the wild represents years of research, collaboration, habitat restoration and careful conservation work.”

Researchers at work with the snakes in wetlands. _Credit: San Francisco Zoo_

The story of why the San Francisco garter snake is under such acute threat is a familiar one: Their habitat is disappearing. The living conditions the species relies on are very specific: They need ponds or other bodies of freshwater to find food, plus hillsides for basking and mating as well as rodent burrows for taking cover in the winter.

That particular mix is rarer than ever due to human development, and most suitable sites for the snake are now on private land. Case in point: The largest population is currently in a protected site close to San Francisco International Airport.

Drought, disease, invasive species, and illegal poaching have also put San Francisco garter snake numbers at critically low levels, making the zoo’s conservation efforts vital for the survival of the species. This year, another 130 baby garter snakes have been born at the zoo, and the plan is to release them in 2027, alongside efforts to restore suitable habitats and improve population monitoring.

“This species is special in many ways, but unfortunately its critical status isn’t unique,” Midpen wildlife ecologist Ariel Starr said in a [statement](https://www.sfzoo.org/a-new-generation-of-san-francisco-garter-snakes-returns-to-the-wild/). “The success of this project and the associated research will not only benefit the San Francisco garter snake but will also hopefully inform the recovery of many imperiled reptile species.”

By giving these reptiles a small head start, the goal is to establish at least 10 viable, self-sustaining populations—or enough to finally remove the species from the endangered list. ![Image 1](https://lede-admin.nautil.us/wp-content/uploads/sites/70/sites/3/nautilus/nautilus-favicon-14.png?fm=png)

title: Can “GTA V” Help Scientists Model Climate Change in L.A.?
content:
You can’t turn your head without seeing an advertisement for _Grand Theft Auto VI_. The ad blitz is reaching a crescendo because the highly anticipated eighth installment in the Rockstar Games franchise drops tomorrow, 13 years after the release of its predecessor, _GTA V_. And after such a long wait, the pressure to deliver is sky high.

After all, _GTA V_ featured a meticulous and immersive recreation of Los Angeles (called Los Santos) based on field research, satellite maps, census data, and more. And Rockstar’s remarkable level of detail has stood the test of time, with many players returning to the game while they wait for the sequel. Climate scientists are apparently no different. In a new study published in _Geoscience Communication_, a team of researchers used the fictional city of Los Santos to model rising sea levels.

**Read more: “**[**Playing Video Games Makes Us Fully Human**](https://nautil.us/playing-video-games-makes-us-fully-human-237447)**”**

“Many games have now advanced graphically to such an extent that they can reproduce real-world locations almost true-to-life,” study author Paul Nörenberg of Germany’s University of Potsdam said in a statement. “The city is a near-exact replica of the real-life Los Angeles, with all its famous landmarks, neighborhoods, and urban and coastal features.”

So Nörenberg and his colleague Hugues Lantuit of the Alfred Wegener Institute inundated the digital city with a series of floods designed to mimic encroaching sea levels under various scenarios based on projections from the U.N.’s Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change. “In one scenario, greenhouse gas emissions were significantly reduced by robust climate action, and in another, emissions remained high,” Lantuit explained.

The high-emission scenario showed the surrounding coastline creeping into Los Santos and water levels rising almost eight feet by the year 2100. By the simulated year 2300, the water level rose another nine feet, knocking out the city’s sewage treatment plants and gasworks, before finally topping out at almost 27 feet by the year 2500. According to their analysis, close to seven percent of Los Santos was lost to the ocean.

The scenario where emissions come under tighter control was a little less dire. In those simulations, the water level only rose seven to nine feet by the year 2500 with a land loss hovering around two percent. Under this model, coastal towns and beaches suffered the brunt of the damage, but key infrastructure located farther inland remained untouched (good news for fans of _GTA V’s_ airport quests).

The researchers also compared their simulations of a flooded Los Santos to models of scientifically documented flood risks in the real City of Angels. They were a close match. “The virtual environment of _GTA V_ is therefore not only visually reminiscent of Los Angeles. Its landscape is precise and detailed enough to be used for a scientific analysis of climate impacts,” Lantuit said.

Why, though, focus on a made-up city like Los Santos in the first place?

According to the team, simulating environments people have an emotional attachment to may make the effects of climate change more tangible to them. “If this familiar, personally explored virtual landscape changes, players can engage with the effects of climate change on an emotional level,” Nörenberg said. “This can bridge a gap in a way that conventional visualizations, such as models or maps, struggle to achieve.”

It’s possible people have a stronger attachment to a fictional (albeit accurate) representation of a city than they do the real thing. It may sound bleak, but _GTA V_ is the second best-selling video game of all time, with over 225 million copies sold—or over 20 times the population of Los Angeles County.

And _GTA VI_ may shatter that record. If so, a new generation could develop a connection to the game’s setting, Vice City. Based on over a decade of research, Vice City is an even more detailed recreation of Miami, Florida, another urban area threatened by climate change. ![Image 1](https://lede-admin.nautil.us/wp-content/uploads/sites/70/sites/3/nautilus/nautilus-favicon-14.png?fm=png)

title: Homo Erectus Adopted a Jungle Lifestyle 200,000 Years Ago
content:
We like to think of ourselves as the pinnacle of hominin evolution (after all, we went to the moon). But if we’re using “length of time on Earth” as our measuring stick, _Homo erectus_ has us beat cold. First popping up on the scene around 2 million years ago, this particular human ancestor was still traveling the globe a scant 100,000 years ago (along with the brand new _Homo sapiens_). Now, [two](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41586-026-11155-6)[studies](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41586-026-11271-3) published today are revealing a new chapter in the species’ life—it’s time roaming the jungles of prehistoric China.

_Homo erectus_ reached China roughly 1.8 million years ago, but it was thought to have vanished from the region by around 400,000 years ago. Encroaching tropical rainforests—dense, complex, and dangerous habitats for our savanna-born kin—were thought to have played a role in its disappearance. But that might not be true. According to the studies, _H. erectus_ survived, living in the jungles as late as 324,000 and 184,000 years ago.

**Read more: “**[**We Now Know What Denisovans Looked Like**](https://nautil.us/we-now-know-what-denisovans-looked-like-1286027)**”**

“This is a fascinating discovery because it confirms the presence of _Homo erectus_ in a location we weren’t expecting and at a time we hadn’t considered,” study author and geochronologist Kira Westaway of Australia’s Macquarie University explained in a [statement](https://www.eurekalert.org/news-releases/1151969). “This has huge implications for the timeline of _Homo erectus_ as we attempt to understand the causes of its extinction.”

The dating evidence comes from eight teeth found in two limestone caves in China’s Guangxi province investigated by an international team of researchers representing a variety of paleo- fields. An assemblage of fossilized bones discovered alongside the teeth was dominated by forest-dwelling fauna like orangutans, tapirs, and _Stegodon_, an extinct elephant-like mammal. Per their isotopic analysis, the bones and the teeth shared similar ratios of carbon, indicating _H. erectus_ had been using similar sources of food as the others.

“Teeth can record the environments in which animals and humans lived,” study author Nicolas Bourgon of the Max Planck Institute of Geoanthropology said. “In this case, the animal teeth and the _Homo erectus_ teeth are telling the same story—these individuals were part of a rainforest ecosystem.”

So _H. erectus_ was more than just a jungle tourist, but that doesn’t mean these resourceful hominins didn’t get around. Analysis of strontium isotopes in four of the teeth showed signs their owners ranged farther afield in their youth, with some ratios matching areas as far away as northern Vietnam (although the researchers call this finding “tentative”).

Importantly, the researchers say the evidence only points to _H. erectus_ surviving in the jungles and that they may not have thrived there. Still, the findings suggest adaptability was key to our longest-lived ancestor’s resilience. “These findings change how we think about _Homo erectus_,” study author Yingqi Zhang of the Chinese Academy of Sciences said. “Finding _Homo erectus_ evidence for the first time amongst a rainforest fauna challenges all our assumptions about their ability to adapt to environmental changes.”

You don’t last two million years on prehistoric Earth without a few tricks up your sleeve. ![Image 1](https://lede-admin.nautil.us/wp-content/uploads/sites/70/sites/3/nautilus/nautilus-favicon-14.png?fm=png)

title: The Speech Patterns of Psychoses
content:
In his 1955 book _The Psychoses,_ French psychoanalyst Jacques Lacan famously argued that someone in the throes of psychosis often feels “possessed by language.” Lacan’s argument stemmed in part from an analysis of the memoirs of Daniel Paul Schreber, a 19th century German judge, who was institutionalized for close to a decade following a mental breakdown and who suffered florid hallucinations and delusions.

Lacan and Schreber both documented in vivid detail the moment in psychosis when one’s sentences become unmoored from reality. What often fills these interruptions, Lacan noticed, are wild linguistic inventions: rigid repetitive chants and neologisms with private and obscure meanings. Schreber himself coined terms such as “soul murder,“ or “miracled-up“ to describe his precarious reality. Today, clinical assessments of people with psychosis often use phrases such as “word salad,“ or “clang associations“ to describe their somersaulting patterns of speech.

**Read more:**[**“The Faulty Weathermen of the Mind”**](https://nautil.us/the-faulty-weathermen-of-the-mind-386474)

But while the connection between psychosis and language has been well documented for decades, measuring these critical moments of linguistic unraveling has remained an elusive project, argues McGill University psychiatrist Lena Palaniyappan. He has been working to address this breach for a decade. In 2021, Palaniyappan put together a consortium called DISCOURSE that now comprises more than 390 members across six continents. Together, they are building the first global bank of the speech patterns, word choices, and voice features of people suffering from psychosis so that they can serve as objective markers of illness progression.

I spoke via email with Palaniyappan about how his childhood ambition to become a writer shaped his interest in the language of psychosis, why these moments of disorganized thinking are more important for our understanding of the illness than bizarre delusions, and why there is no such thing as a definitive account of psychosis.

**You recently told****_Genomic Press_****that one of the things that brought you into the field of psychiatry was taking the antipsychotic haloperidol yourself as a personal challenge. What was the challenge you set for yourself, and what was the experience of taking haloperidol like?**

I should say at the outset that this was not an experiment. It was a piece of student foolishness, and I would not recommend it to anybody. I was a medical student at Stanley Medical College Hospital in Chennai, sitting in on an outpatient clinic, and what struck me was the sameness of it. Patient after patient, whatever they had arrived with, left with haloperidol. And a good many of them were told, more or less in passing, that they would be taking it for the rest of their lives.

That seemed to me an extraordinary thing to say to a person or carer carrying a lot of uncertainty in their minds. We were asking people to live inside a drug indefinitely, one which, I found during a lunchtime chat, that not one of us in that room had the faintest idea what that was like. So I took some, to find out.

**When you were young, you wanted to be a writer, but out of practicality, you chose medicine instead. How does that interest in language and writing shape your study of the language of psychosis?**

I wanted to be a writer and I did medicine instead, which is roughly what a family of teachers in Tamil Nadu expects of a boy who turns out to be good at examinations. When I was much younger, I had the notion that universities existed chiefly to produce writers, who would then go away and do the work that helps the universities to stack their libraries. It took me some years to discover that this does not appear in any prospectus. You can imagine my disappointment.

What I did not foresee was that the two things would meet. Psychiatry is the one branch of medicine in which the instrument of examination is a conversation. A cardiologist listens to a heart; I listen to sentences. And if you have spent your adolescence being interested in how sentences work, you start to notice things in a clinic that are otherwise easy to miss: not what the person is saying, but the route the sentence takes, and whether it ever arrives. The literary habit turns out to be a clinical one, which is a convenient discovery for somebody who had already made his choice.

**What are some of the telltale signs of psychosis in speech?**

Far less dramatic than people expect. Nobody comes in speaking in tongues. What you notice is a sentence that sets off in one direction and quietly arrives somewhere else, with no sign from the speaker that anything peculiar has happened.

You notice pronouns with nothing behind them, so that “he” and “they” and “it” float free of any particular person. You notice answers that are perfectly grammatical and almost entirely empty: a great deal of language carrying very little cargo. And you notice the reverse as well—speech that dries up, where the words are few and arrive slowly, as though each one had to be fetched from a long way off.

The unsettling part is how ordinary each instance looks on its own. All of us derail—a good reason never to give more than 20 minutes to a speaker for any academic talks. All of us produce the occasional sentence that gets lost in the post, particularly before coffee. It is the rate at which it happens, and the fact that the speaker does not notice, that carries the information.

**Why have psychiatrists failed to measure these slips and drifts reliably so far?**

Three reasons, all of them unglamorous. The first is that we never agreed what to sample. A blood test has a tube. Thought disorder has whatever the patient happened to say in the twelve minutes you had with them, to a stranger, in a room they did not choose, possibly in their second or third language. Alter any one of those and you alter the speech.

The second is that we asked clinicians to do arithmetic in their heads. The classic scales require you to hold 40 minutes of conversation in memory and emerge with a single number between nought and four. Human beings—especially us psychiatrists—are not built for that, and two conscientious clinicians will honestly disagree.

The third is that the interesting events are rare. If a feature occurs three times in an hour, a short interview will often catch none of them. The scale then scores zero, looks beautifully reliable, and tells you nothing whatsoever. Rarity and reliability are very easily confused, and the confusion has cost us decades.

**Why are these moments of disorganized thinking more important for our understanding of the illness than the hallucination or the bizarre delusion?**

Because the hallucination and the delusion are, in a sense, content. They tell you what a person is experiencing, or what they have come to believe. Disorganization we see in the language is about the machinery, and the machinery is the thing we are actually trying to understand.

There are blunter reasons, too. Disorganized thinking predicts, better than the other symptoms do, whether somebody will hold a job, keep their friends, or follow what is being said around a table. It is also the symptom our drugs touch least. We have spent seventy years becoming steadily better at quietening voices and have left the disorganization more or less where we found it. That ought to trouble us rather more than it does.

And it is the part of the illness that is taken most quietly, because patients do not come to us describing it. A voice is an intruder, and an intruder can be described. Your own sentence that left its destination several clauses ago cannot be reported, because from the inside it did not happen.

This reminds me of Anne Sexton who wrote of words, “Yet often they fail me. I have so much I want to say, so many stories, images, proverbs, etc. But the words aren’t good enough, the wrong ones kiss me.” How many of us can be that articulate when words are failing us?

**Your biggest ambition you have said is finding ways to prevent mental illness from taking hold in young people. Do you have some clues about how to solve this problem? And how might your current work on listening to psychosis help?**

The ambition is less heroic than it sounds. I would like us to be able to postpone this illness, or to soften it, in young people who at present are told to come back when they are worse. The obstacle is really the arithmetic. You cannot run a prevention trial for something you cannot measure cheaply, repeatedly, and in the same way in Chennai as in Montreal.

At the moment, assessing a young person’s thinking takes a trained clinician the better part of an hour, which means it happens perhaps twice a year, which means we are watching a slow illness through two snapshots and guessing at everything in between. Speech is the obvious way out of that, for the unromantic reason that it is free. People produce it anyway, it can be sampled as often as you like, and nobody has to be poked with a needle to get it.

If ordinary conversations could be harnessed to tell us which young people are drifting and which are steady, prevention stops being a slogan and becomes a trial somebody can actually run. That is the whole bridge between the listening and the ambition. The rest is engineering.

**Have any writers you have read faithfully captured the experience of psychosis?**

Psychosis is not one experience that various writers have rendered with varying accuracy. It is a very large number of quite different experiences, and the moment any single account becomes the prototype, everybody whose illness fails to match it is told, usually by implication, that they are doing it wrong. So what I recommend is not a book but a series: the [“First Person Accounts” in _Schizophrenia Bulletin_](https://academic.oup.com/schizophreniabulletin/pages/first_person_accounts). They are short. They are written by people who have lived it rather than people who have studied it. And there are a great many of them. You get the one thing no single memoir can give you, which is the range. Read five and you stop hunting for the definitive account. Read twenty and you understand why there is not one.

**If you were to recommend one book about psychosis or mental illness to a parent of a child suffering with the disease, what would you select?**

I am going to dodge this one a little, because I think there is a better question hiding inside it. There are a great many good books, and which one I would hand over changes entirely with the problem in front of me. A parent frightened by a first episode needs something quite different from a parent two years in who is exhausted and angry, and different again from a parent whose child is well and bored and wondering whether to stop the tablets. One title for all of that would be like one dose for all of that.

So here is what I would say instead. When you ask your doctor for a prescription, ask them for a book as well. Bibliotherapy is extraordinarily underused in mental health. A book is the only prescription with no interactions, and is one of the very few things we can offer that treats the family and not only the patient.

**What books are you reading now, or are sitting on your bedside table?**

Sadly, I collect more than I can read. Two of the pile, however, are genuinely in progress right now. One is Arundhati Roy’s _Mother Mary Comes to Me_, her memoir of her mother, which is the most uncomfortable sort of love letter and much the better for it. The other is Karl Deisseroth’s _Projections_, which is the opposite kind of book altogether. ![Image 1](https://lede-admin.nautil.us/wp-content/uploads/sites/70/sites/3/nautilus/nautilus-favicon-14.png?fm=png)
